metadata.title: EDF-Like Scheduling for Self-Suspending Real-Time Tasks

extraction_notes.note: EL scheduling is the uniprocessor version of GEL (Erickson & Anderson); marked external although the paper restates it formally as Definition 1.
Proof-sketch rule asks for rigor semi_formal on the sketch, while the rigor rule (and the finishing step) excludes proofs; rigor omitted, sketches marked by alternative proves edges.
pseudocode_steps returned an empty statement for the final \Return line of both algorithms; replaced by the verbatim line text. Comment-only \triangleright lines of Algorithm 2 were dropped.
Implementation descriptions for RTEMS and LITMUS^RT (Section 5), the notation table, figure-only content and roadmap/motivation paragraphs were not extracted.
Proof of Lemma 21 is separated from the lemma by an intuition paragraph (PP18), so its proves edge is added by hand.

ChenECRTS2016-Partition.text: abstract = { Partitioned multiprocessor scheduling has been widely accepted in academia and industry to statically assign and partition real-time tasks onto identical multiprocessor systems. This paper studies fixed-priority partitioned multiprocessor scheduling for sporadic real-time systems, in which deadline-monotonic scheduling is applied on each processor. Prior to this paper, the best known results are by Fisher, Baruah, and Baker with speedup factors $4-\frac{2}{M}$ and $3-\frac{1}{M}$ for arbitrary-deadline and constrained-deadline sporadic real-time task systems, respectively, where $M$ is the number of processors. We show that a greedy mapping strategy has a speedup factor $3-\frac{1}{M}$ when considering task systems with arbitrary deadlines. Such a factor holds for polynomial-time schedulability tests and exponential-time (exact) schedulability tests. Moreover, we also improve the speedup factor to $2.84306$ when considering constrained-deadline task systems. We also provide tight examples when the fitting strategy in the mapping stage is arbitrary and $M$ is sufficiently large. For both constrained- and arbitrary-deadline task systems, the analytical result surprisingly shows that using exact tests does not gain theoretical benefits (with respect to speedup factors) if the speedup factor analysis is oblivious of the particular fitting strategy used.}, author = {Chen, Jian-Jia}, booktitle = {Euromicro Conference on Real-Time Systems (ECRTS)}, date-added = {2016-08

Chen:RTS2016-Federated.text: abstract = { In the federated scheduling approaches in multiprocessor systems, a task either 1) is restricted to execute sequentially on a single processor or 2) has exclusive access to the assigned processors. There have been several positive results to conduct good federated scheduling policies, which have constant speedup factors with respect to any optimal federated scheduling algorithm. This paper answers an open question: ``For constrained-deadline task systems with directed acyclic graph (DAG) dependency structures, do federated scheduling policies have a constant speedup factor with respect to any optimal scheduling algorithm?'' The answer is ``No!'' This paper presents an example, which demonstrates that any federated scheduling algorithm has a speedup factor of at least $\Omega(\min\{M, N\})$ with respect to any optimal scheduling algorithm, where $N$ is the number of tasks and $M$ is the number of processors.}, author = {Chen, Jian-Jia}, date-added = {2016-08-15 14:37:17 +0000}, date-modified = {2017-04-25 14:49:00 +0000}, doi = {10.1007/s11241-016-9255-2}, journal = {Real-Time Systems}, month = {November}, number = {6}, pages = {833--838}, title = {Federated Scheduling Admits No Constant Speedup Factors for Constrained-Deadline DAG Task Systems}, volume = {52}, year = {2016}, bdsk-url-1 = {http://doi.org/10.1007/s11241-016-9255-2} }

IPL2016-speedup.text: abstract = {In this paper, we investigate the quality of several linear-time schedulability tests for preemptive and non-preemptive fixed-priority scheduling of uniprocessor systems. The metric used to assess the quality of these tests is the resource augmentation bound commonly known as the processor speedup factor. The speedup factor of a schedulability test corresponds to the smallest factor by which the processing speed of a uniprocessor needs to be increased such that any task set that is feasible under an optimal preemptive (non-preemptive) work-conserving scheduling algorithm is guaranteed to be schedulable with preemptive (non-preemptive) fixed priority scheduling if this scheduling test is used, assuming an appropriate priority assignment. We show the surprising result that the exact speedup factors for Deadline Monotonic (DM) priority assignment combined with sufficient linear-time schedulability tests for implicit-, constrained-, and arbitrary-deadline task sets are the same as those obtained for optimal priority assignment policies combined with exact schedulability tests. Thus in terms of the speedup-factors required, there is no penalty in using DM priority assignment and simple linear schedulability tests. }, author = {Georg von der Br\"uggen and Jian-Jia Chen and Robert I. Davis and Wen-Hung Huang}, date-added = {2016-08-12 13:27:07 +0000}, date-modified = {2017-04-25 15:01:42 +0000}, doi = {10.1016/j.ipl.2016.08.001}, journal = {Information Processing Letters

LunnissLITES2014.text: abstract = {In multitasking real-time systems, the choice of scheduling algorithm is an important factor to ensure that response time requirements are met while maximising limited system resources. Two popular scheduling algorithms include fixed priority (FP) and earliest deadline first (EDF). While they have been studied in great detail before, they have not been compared when taking into account cache related pre-emption delays (CRPD). Memory and cache are split into a number of blocks containing instructions and data. During a pre-emption, cache blocks from the pre-empting task can evict those of the pre-empted task. When the pre-empted task is resumed, if it then has to re-load the evicted blocks, CRPD are introduced which then affect the schedulability of the task. In this paper we compare FP and EDF scheduling algorithms in the presence of CRPD using the state-of-the-art CRPD analysis. We find that when CRPD is accounted for, the performance gains offered by EDF over FP, while still notable, are diminished. Furthermore, we find that under scenarios that cause relatively high CRPD, task layout optimisation techniques can be applied to allow FP to schedule tasksets at a similar processor utilisation to EDF. Thus making the choice of the task layout in memory as important as the choice of scheduling algorithm. This is very relevant for industry, as it is much cheaper and simpler to adjust the task layout through the linker than it is to switch the scheduling algorithm.}, a

10.1023/B:TIME.0000048932.30002.d9.text: author = {Buttazzo, Giorgio C.}, title = {Rate Monotonic vs. EDF: Judgment Day}, year = {2005}, issue_date = {January 2005}, publisher = {Kluwer Academic Publishers}, address = {USA}, volume = {29}, number = {1}, issn = {0922-6443}, url = {https://doi.org/10.1023/B:TIME.0000048932.30002.d9}, doi = {10.1023/B:TIME.0000048932.30002.d9}, abstract = {Since the first results published in 1973 by Liu and Layland on the Rate Monotonic (RM) and Earliest Deadline First (EDF) algorithms, a lot of progress has been made in the schedulability analysis of periodic task sets. Unfortunately, many misconceptions still exist about the properties of these two scheduling methods, which usually tend to favor RM more than EDF. Typical wrong statements often heard in technical conferences and even in research papers claim that RM is easier to analyze than EDF, it introduces less runtime overhead, it is more predictable in overload conditions, and causes less jitter in task execution.Since the above statements are either wrong, or not precise, it is time to clarify these issues in a systematic fashion, because the use of EDF allows a better exploitation of the available resources and significantly improves system's performance.This paper compares RM against EDF under several aspects, using existing theoretical results, specific simulation experiments, or simple counterexamples to show that many common beliefs are either false or only restricted to specific situations.}, journal = {Real-Time Syst.},

10.1145/2597457.2597458.text: author = {Davis, Robert I.}, title = {A Review of Fixed Priority and EDF Scheduling for Hard Real-Time Uniprocessor Systems}, year = {2014}, issue_date = {February 2014}, publisher = {Association for Computing Machinery}, address = {New York, NY, USA}, volume = {11}, number = {1}, url = {https://doi.org/10.1145/2597457.2597458}, doi = {10.1145/2597457.2597458}, abstract = {This paper was written to accompany a talk at the ETR Summer School in Toulouse 2013. It provides a background and primer to scheduling and schedulability analysis for hard real-time single processor systems. The paper focuses on the two main scheduling algorithms used: Fixed Priority and Earliest Deadline First. The paper has two broad aims: Firstly to provide a guide to the fundamental results for these real-time scheduling algorithms. Secondly to provide a brief review of extensions aimed at (i) limiting the effects and overheads of pre-emption and (ii) accounting for the effects of pre-emptions; specifically cache related pre-emption delays. The paper also briefly looks back at success stories in real-time scheduling, and forwards at the current hot topics in this research area.}, journal = {SIGBED Rev.}, month = feb, pages = {8–19}, numpages = {12}, keywords = {EDF, schedulability analysis, limited pre-emption, fixed priority, scheduling, survey, cache-related pre-emption delays, single processor, real-time, uniprocessor} }

nodes.name: Self-suspending task
nodes.statement:
For \emph{self-suspending} task sets, a job may release
    its occupation of the processor before being completed, and may
    wait, for instance due to computation offloading or hardware
    acceleration, until the requested service is completed.
nodes.statement_short: In self-suspending task sets a job may release the processor before completion and wait for an external service.

nodes.name: Segmented self-suspension model
nodes.statement:
In the segmented self-suspension model, the sequence of execution and suspension behavior of all jobs is predefined for each task.
	More specifically, for each segment a suspension or execution upper bound is given and the number of segments is fixed.
nodes.origin_citation: Bletsas & Audsley 2005; Chen & Liu 2014; et al.
nodes.statement_short: Each task has a predefined sequence of execution and suspension segments with given upper bounds.

nodes.name: Dynamic self-suspension model
nodes.statement:
In the dynamic self-suspension model, the segmented structure is
    not predefined. 	The jobs of one task may suspend as often and
    as long as the maximum suspension time is not exceeded.
nodes.origin_citation: Audsley & Bletsas 2004; Chen et al. 2016; et al.
nodes.statement_short: Jobs may suspend arbitrarily often and long as long as the maximum suspension time is respected.

nodes.name: Task-Level Fixed-Priority (TFP) scheduling
nodes.statement: In Task-Level \emph{Fixed-Priority} (TFP) scheduling algorithms, the priority is assigned to tasks, i.e., if one task has a higher priority than another task, then all of its jobs are favored to be executed.
differentia: the priority is assigned to tasks

nodes.name: Task-level dynamic-priority scheduling
nodes.statement: In task-level dynamic-priority scheduling algorithms, the priority of the jobs of one task may differ at different time instants.

nodes.name: Earliest-Deadline-First (EDF)
nodes.statement: The study of suspension-aware schedulability tests for task-level dynamic-priority scheduling algorithms has been limited to the Earliest-Deadline-First (EDF) algorithm, in which the priority of a job is specified by its absolute deadline.
differentia: the priority of a job is specified by its absolute deadline

nodes.name: Window-constrained schedulers
nodes.statement: The category of \emph{window-constrained} schedulers, where at each time job priorities are assigned according to a \emph{priority point (PP)}, has been proposed in the literature~\cite{DBLP:conf/rtss/LeontyevA07} originally for multiprocessor scheduling to provide general tardiness bounds.
differentia: at each time job priorities are assigned according to a \emph{priority point (PP)}

nodes.name: Global EDF-Like (GEL) scheduling
nodes.statement: Recent results~\cite{DBLP:conf/ecrts/EricksonA12} consider \emph{Global EDF-Like (GEL)} scheduling algorithms, where the priority point of the window-constrained scheduler is induced by the job release and a task specific \emph{relative priority point}.
differentia: the priority point of the window-constrained scheduler is induced by the job release and a task specific \emph{relative priority point}

nodes.name: No constant speedup factors under suspension
nodes.statement: Furthermore, Chen~\cite{RTSS2016-suspension} proved that TFP, EDF, Least-Laxity-First (LLF), and Earliest-Deadline-Zero-Laxity~(EDZL) scheduling algorithms do not have constant speedup factors when the suspension cannot be sped up.
assumptions: the suspension cannot be sped up
conclusions: TFP, EDF, Least-Laxity-First (LLF), and Earliest-Deadline-Zero-Laxity~(EDZL) scheduling algorithms do not have constant speedup factors

nodes.name: Self-suspending sporadic task set
nodes.statement: In this work, we consider a set $\Tbb=\{\tau_1, \dots, \tau_n\}$ of $n$ independent self-suspending sporadic real-time tasks, in a uniprocessor system.
nodes.statement_short: The task set $\Tbb$ of $n$ independent self-suspending sporadic tasks on one processor.

nodes.name: Self-suspending sporadic task parameters
nodes.statement: Each task $\tau_i,~i \in \{1,\dots, n\}$ is described by a $4$-tuple $\tau_i = (C_i, S_i, D_i, T_i)$, composed of worst-case execution time (WCET) $C_i \in [0,D_i]$, maximum suspension time $S_i\geq 0$, relative deadline $D_i\geq0$ and minimum inter-arrival time $T_i>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Task $\tau_i=(C_i,S_i,D_i,T_i)$: WCET, maximum suspension, relative deadline, minimum inter-arrival time.

nodes.name: Jobs and release times
nodes.statement: The task $\tau_i$ releases infinitely many jobs, denoted by $\tau_{i,j},~j \in \Nbb$, at time $r_{i,j},~j \in \Nbb$.

nodes.name: Sporadic release separation
nodes.statement: Job releases are separated by at least $T_i$ time units, i.e., $r_{i,j+1} \geq r_{i,j} + T_i$.

nodes.name: Job execution time and absolute deadline
nodes.statement: Each job $\tau_{i,j}$ has to be executed for a certain amount of time $c_{i,j} \in [0,C_i]$ until its absolute deadline $d_{i,j} = r_{i,j} + D_i$.

nodes.name: Dynamic self-suspension of jobs
nodes.statement: In addition, each job suspends itself dynamically, i.e., it may suspend itself as often as desired without exceeding the maximum suspension time $S_i$.

nodes.name: Utilization
nodes.statement: We denote by $U_i := \frac{C_i}{T_i}$ the utilization of $\tau_i$ and by $U := \sum_{i=1}^{n} U_i$ the total utilization of $\Tbb$.

nodes.name: Constrained-deadline task system
nodes.statement:
A task set $\Tbb$ is a \emph{constrained-deadline} task system if
$D_i \leq T_i$ is ensured for every $\tau_i \in \Tbb$.

nodes.name: Arbitrary-deadline task system
nodes.statement:
Otherwise, it is an
\emph{arbitrary-deadline} task system.

nodes.name: Continuous time
nodes.statement: We assume a model where time is continuous.

nodes.name: Scheduling algorithm
nodes.statement:
A scheduling algorithm $\Acal$ specifies the execution behavior of jobs on the processor.
More specifically, they determine at each time, which of the jobs in the ready queue is scheduled by the processor.

nodes.name: Start and finish times
nodes.statement: In a certain schedule we denote for each job $\tau_{i,j}$ start $s_{i,j}$ and finish $f_{i,j}$ of its execution.

nodes.name: Finished by time t
nodes.statement: We say that a job $\tau_{i,j}$ is \emph{finished by} time $t$, if $f_{i,j}\leq t$.

nodes.name: Response time
nodes.statement: The length of the time interval from release to finish of a job $\tau_{i,j}$ is called the {response time} $R_{i,j} = f_{i,j}-r_{i,j}$.

nodes.name: Worst-case response time
nodes.statement: Of special interest is the \emph{worst-case response time} $R_i = \sup_j R_{i,j}$ of a task $\tau_i$.

nodes.name: Feasible schedule
nodes.statement: A schedule is \emph{feasible}, if all jobs finish before or at their absolute deadline, i.e., $f_{i,j} \leq d_{i,j}$ for all $\tau_{i,j}$ or $R_i \leq D_i$ for all $\tau_i$.

nodes.name: Schedulable task set
nodes.statement: A task set is \emph{schedulable} by a scheduling algorithm $\Acal$ if for each job sequence released by $\Tbb$, $\Acal$ creates a feasible schedule.
differentia: for each job sequence released by $\Tbb$, $\Acal$ creates a feasible schedule

nodes.name: Preemptive work-conserving scheduling
nodes.statement: In this work, we only consider preemptive, work-conserving scheduling, where job execution may be preempted to execute another job, and the processor executes a job whenever there is one in the ready queue.

nodes.name: Number sets
nodes.statement: In the following, we denote by $\Nbb$, $\Nbb_0$, and $\Rbb$ the sets of natural numbers, non-negative integers, and real numbers.

nodes.name: EDF-Like (EL) scheduling
nodes.statement:
In EDF-Like (EL) scheduling, the priority of each job $\tau_{i,j}$ is based on a job-specific \emph{priority point} (PP) $\pi_{i,j} \in \Rbb$.
More specifically, a job $\tau_{i,j}$ has higher priority than $\tau_{i',j'}$ if  $\pi_{i,j}<\pi_{i',j'}$.
nodes.statement_short: In EL scheduling each job has a priority point $\pi_{i,j}$; smaller priority point means higher priority.

nodes.name: Relative priority point
nodes.statement: The priority point is induced by the release of the job and a task specific paramater $\Pi_i$ denoted by \emph{relative priority point}, i.e., $\pi_{i,j} = r_{i,j} + \Pi_i$.

nodes.name: Priority assignment in EL scheduling
nodes.statement: Let $\tau_{i,j}$ and $\tau_{i',j'}$ be two different jobs obtained by tasks $\tau_i$ and $\tau_{i'}$ in~$\Tbb$. Furthermore, let $\Pi_i$ and $\Pi_{i'}$ be the relative priority points of $\tau_i$ and $\tau_{i'}$. The job $\tau_{i,j}$ has \emph{higher priority} than $\tau_{i',j'}$ if \begin{equation} \pi_{i,j} < \pi_{i',j'} \end{equation} for the priority points $\pi_{i,j} = r_{i,j} + \Pi_i$ and $\pi_{i',j'} = r_{i',j'} + \Pi_{i'}$. If the priority points coincide, i.e., $\pi_{i,j} = \pi_{i',j'}$, then the tie is broken arbitrarily.
nodes.statement_short: Job $\tau_{i,j}$ has higher priority than $\tau_{i',j'}$ if $r_{i,j}+\Pi_i < r_{i',j'}+\Pi_{i'}$; ties broken arbitrarily.
nodes.label: defn:priority_rp

nodes.name: EL scheduling dispatch
nodes.statement:
Under an assignment of relative priority points $(\Pi_1, \dots, \Pi_n)$, when a job is added to the ready queue, the new highest-priority job is determined and executed.
Whenever a job finishes or suspends itself, it is removed from the ready queue and a new highest-priority job has to be determined and is executed.
nodes.statement_short: Dispatch rule: on every arrival, completion or suspension, (re)select and run the highest-priority ready job.

nodes.name: Example EL schedule of two tasks
nodes.statement: The right hand side of Figure~\ref{fig:exmample_notation} shows an example schedule obtained by the task set $\Tbb=\{\tau_1,\tau_2\}$, with $\tau_1=(C_1=2, S_1=0, D_1=5, T_1=5)$ and $\tau_2=(C_2=7, S_2=3, D_2=16, T_2=16)$, when using EL scheduling with relative priority points $(\Pi_1=4,\Pi_2=10)$.
nodes.statement_short: Two-task set scheduled by EL with $\Pi_1=4$, $\Pi_2=10$ yields a feasible schedule.

nodes.name: Intra-task FIFO execution of jobs
nodes.statement:
We consider that the jobs of a task $\tau_i$ must be executed one
after another in a FIFO manner. If a job $\tau_{i,j}$ of task
$\tau_i$ does not finish execution before the next job
$\tau_{i,j+1}$ of $\tau_i$ is released, job $\tau_{i,j+1}$
cannot be executed even if the processor idles. That is, the
EL scheduling algorithm has to handle this situation as
follows: 1) It sets the priority of the job $\tau_{i,j+1}$ to
$r_{i,j+1} + \Pi_i$ when it arrives at $r_{i,j+1}$, but 2) this
job is only eligible for execution (i.e., ready to be executed) after
all jobs of $\tau_i$ released prior to $\tau_{i,j+1}$ finish execution.
nodes.statement_short: Jobs of the same task execute in FIFO order; a job is eligible only after all earlier jobs of its task finish.

nodes.name: EL scheduling is job-level fixed-priority
nodes.statement: EDF-Like (EL) scheduling algorithms are Job-Level Fixed-Priority (JFP) scheduling algorithms, i.e., if one job has higher priority than another job, then it has higher priority at all times.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
conclusions: EDF-Like (EL) scheduling algorithms are Job-Level Fixed-Priority (JFP) scheduling algorithms

nodes.name: Proof that EL is JFP
nodes.statement:
This is due to the priority definition by comparison of priority points.
Since the priority point of a job does not change once it is assigned, the priorities of jobs are fixed after they are released.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: Priority points never change after release, so job priorities are fixed.

nodes.name: EL covers EDF, EQDF, SAEDF and FIFO
nodes.statement:
However, EL scheduling covers many of those JFP scheduling algorithms.
These are for example: 
\begin{itemize}
	\item Earliest-Deadline-First (EDF)~\cite{liu73scheduling} ($\Pi_i = D_i$)
	\item Earliest-Quasi-Deadline-First (EQDF)~\cite{DBLP:conf/rtas/BackCS12} \\($\Pi_i = D_i + \lambda C_i$ for some predefined $\lambda \in \Rbb$) 
	\item Suspension-aware variations of EDF (SAEDF)\\($\Pi_i = D_i + \lambda S_i$ for some predefined $\lambda \in \Rbb$) 
	\item First-In-First-Out (FIFO) ($\Pi_i = 0$)
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: EDF ($\Pi_i=D_i$), EQDF ($D_i+\lambda C_i$), SAEDF ($D_i+\lambda S_i$) and FIFO ($\Pi_i=0$) are EL configurations.
conclusions: EL scheduling covers many of those JFP scheduling algorithms

nodes.name: Tasks ordered by TFP priority
nodes.statement: For this purpose, we assume that the tasks are ordered by their priorities, i.e., $\tau_k$ has higher priority than $\tau_{k'}$ if and only if $k<k'$, and $\tau_1$ has the highest priority.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling

nodes.name: Given response time bounds K_j
nodes.statement: Furthermore, we assume that a worst-case response time upper bound $K_j$ for each task either for the schedule under EL scheduling or under TFP scheduling is given.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling

nodes.name: TFP not expressible with unbounded response times
nodes.statement:
Please note that the response time 
of tasks may be unbounded and that for such cases a TFP algorithm cannot be treated as EL scheduling algorithm.
However, these cases do not apply in practical scenarios since in real-time systems it is required that the jobs of all tasks finish until their deadline.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling

nodes.name: TFP as EL
nodes.statement: Let $K_1, \dots, K_n \in \Rbb_{\geq 0}$ and $\Pi_i := \sum_{j=1}^{i} K_j$ for $i=1,\dots, n$. If for all $j=1,\dots, n$ the value $K_j$ is an upper bound on the worst-case response time of $\tau_j$ in EL or in TFP, then the schedule of $\Tbb$ under EL and the schedule of $\Tbb$ under TFP coincide.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
also_stated_at: If we set the relative priority point of each task $\tau_i$ to $\Pi_i = \sum_{j=1}^{i} K_j$, then EL and TFP coincide.
assumptions: $K_1, \dots, K_n \in \Rbb_{\geq 0}$ and $\Pi_i := \sum_{j=1}^{i} K_j$ for $i=1,\dots, n$
for all $j=1,\dots, n$ the value $K_j$ is an upper bound on the worst-case response time of $\tau_j$ in EL or in TFP
conclusions: the schedule of $\Tbb$ under EL and the schedule of $\Tbb$ under TFP coincide
nodes.statement_short: With $\Pi_i$ the prefix sums of response-time bounds $K_j$, the EL and TFP schedules coincide.
nodes.label: prop:TFPasEL

nodes.name: Proof of TFP as EL
nodes.statement: For an indirect proof we assume that the schedule of $\Tbb$ under EL and TFP does not coincide. Let $\tau_{k,\ell}$ be the job with the highest priority in the EL schedule, such that the schedule of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ does not coincide under EL and TFP. We define the interval \begin{equation} I := [r_{k,\ell}, r_{k,\ell} + K_k). \end{equation} Let $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}$ and $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}$ be the set of jobs with higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$ under TFP and under EL that are executed during $I$. We will reach a contradiction by showing that $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}=\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}$ and that further the schedule of the jobs in $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}=\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}$ coincides under TFP and under EL scheduling. For that purpose we partition the job sets into three subsets $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}} = \coprod_{i \in \setof{+, -, 0}} \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^i$ and $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}} = \coprod_{i \in \setof{+, -, 0}} \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^i$, where each of them denotes the subset of jobs released by tasks of $\Tbb_{+} = \setof{\tau_{k+1}, \dots, \tau_n}$, $\Tbb_{-} = \setof{\tau_1, \dots, \tau_{k-1}}$ or $\Tbb_{0} = \setof{\tau_k}$. In the following we show that $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^i = \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^i$ for all $i \in \setof{+,-,0}$. \paragraph{$\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^+ = \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^+$} Under TFP, there are no jobs of $\Tbb_{+}$ with higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$, i.e., $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^+ = \emptyset$. Under EL, we choose any job $\tau_{i,j}$, with $\tau_i \in \Tbb_{+}$, that has higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$, i.e., $\pi_{i,j}=r_{i,j} + \Pi_i \leq \pi_{k,\ell} = r_{k,\ell} + \Pi_k$ holds. By subtracting $\Pi_k$ we obtain \begin{equation} r_{i,j} + K_i \leq r_{i,j} + (\Pi_i-\Pi_k) \leq r_{k,\ell}. \end{equation} Since $\tau_{i,j}$ has higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$, by assumption the schedule of $\tau_{i,j}$ coincides under EL and TFP, and we have $f_{i,j} \leq r_{i,j} + K_i$. With Equation~\eqref{eq:pf_prop_TFPasEL_1} we conclude $f_{i,j} \leq r_{k,\ell}$. In particular, the job $\tau_{i,j}$ is not executed during $I$. Since $\tau_{i,j}$ was chosen arbitrarily, this means that $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^+ = \emptyset$ as well. \paragraph{$\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^- = \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^-$} Under TFP and under EL, jobs of the tasks in $\Tbb_{-}$ can only be executed during $I$ if they are released before $r_{k,\ell} + K_k$, i.e., let $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$ be the set of jobs released before $r_{k,\ell} + K_k$ by tasks of $\Tbb_{-}$ then $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^-, \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^- \subseteq \tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$. Under TFP, all jobs in $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$ have higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$ since they are released by the tasks of $\Tbb_{-}$. Under EL, we show the same: Let $\tau_{i,j} \in \tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$, i.e., $r_{i,j} < r_{k,\ell} + K_k$. It directly follows that \begin{equation} \pi_{i,j} = r_{i,j} + \Pi_i < r_{k,\ell} + K_k + \Pi_i \leq r_{k,\ell} + \Pi_k = \pi_{k,\ell}. \end{equation} In particular, $\tau_{i,j}$ has higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$. We have shown that all jobs in $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$ have higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$ under EL and under TFP scheduling. By assumption the schedule of the jobs in $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$ coincides under TFP and EL. Therefore the same jobs of $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$ executed during $I$ under TFP and EL, i.e., $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^- = \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^-$. \paragraph{$\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^0 = \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^0$} Under TFP and under EL, $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^0 := \setof{\tau_{k,1}, \dots, \tau_{k,\ell-1}}$ are the jobs of $\tau_k$ that have higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$, i.e., $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^0, \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^0 \subseteq \tilde{\mathbb{J}}^0$. By assumption, the schedule of the jobs in $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^0$ coincides. Therefore the same jobs of $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^0$ are executed during $I$, i.e., we have $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^0 = \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^0$. We have shown that $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}=\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}$ by the above discussion. Since the schedule of the jobs $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}=\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}$ coincides during $I$, $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is preempted/blocked during the same time intervals under TFP and EL scheduling during $I$. Hence, the schedule of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ during $I$ coincides. Furthermore, since by assumption $K_k$ is an upper bound on the response time under EL or TFP scheduling, the job $\tau_{k,\ell}$ finishes during $I$. This proves that the whole schedule of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ coincides.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction on the highest-priority job whose schedules differ; split higher-priority jobs into lower-, higher- and same-task sets and show each coincides.

nodes.name: Interval I
nodes.statement: I := [r_{k,\ell}, r_{k,\ell} + K_k).
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling

nodes.name: Release bound for lower-priority-task jobs
nodes.statement: r_{i,j} + K_i \leq r_{i,j} + (\Pi_i-\Pi_k) \leq r_{k,\ell}.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.label: eq:pf_prop_TFPasEL_1

nodes.name: Priority point bound for higher-priority-task jobs
nodes.statement: \pi_{i,j} = r_{i,j} + \Pi_i < r_{k,\ell} + K_k + \Pi_i \leq r_{k,\ell} + \Pi_k = \pi_{k,\ell}.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling

nodes.name: Sketch: EL test yields TFP test
nodes.statement:
Even without knowledge about the worst-case response times, we can use a schedulability test based on EL scheduling for TFP scheduling by setting the relative priority points to $\Pi_i = \sum_{j=1}^i D_j$.
If the schedulability test assures that all jobs meet their deadline, then $D_j$ is an upper bound on the worst-case response time.
In this case, the schedule obtained by EL scheduling coincides with the TFP schedule and is feasible.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: Set $\Pi_i=\sum_{j\le i} D_j$; a positive EL test makes $D_j$ response-time bounds, so EL equals TFP.

nodes.name: EL schedulability with deadline prefix sums implies TFP schedulability
nodes.statement: If the task set $\Tbb$ is schedulable under EL with $\Pi_i := \sum_{j=1}^{i} D_j, i=1,\dots, n$, then $\Tbb$ is schedulable under TFP as well.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
assumptions: the task set $\Tbb$ is schedulable under EL with $\Pi_i := \sum_{j=1}^{i} D_j, i=1,\dots, n$
conclusions: $\Tbb$ is schedulable under TFP as well

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4
nodes.statement: If $\Tbb$ is schedulable under EL with the given relative priority points $\Pi_i$, then $D_j$ is an upper bound on the worst-case response time of $\tau_j$ for all $\tau_j \in \Tbb$ under EL scheduling. In this case, by Proposition~\ref{prop:TFPasEL} the schedule under TFP and EL coincide. Therefore, $D_j$ is also an upper bound on the worst-case response time of $\tau_j$ for all $\tau_j \in \Tbb$ under TFP scheduling. Hence, $\Tbb$ is schedulable under TFP as well.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: Deadlines become response-time bounds, so Proposition 3 makes EL and TFP schedules coincide.

nodes.name: Expressiveness of EL between TFP and JFP
nodes.statement: By our discussion in this section, the expressiveness of EDF-Like (EL) scheduling algorithms is between Task-Level Fixed-Priority (TFP) and Job-Level Fixed-Priority (JFP) scheduling.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
conclusions: the expressiveness of EDF-Like (EL) scheduling algorithms is between Task-Level Fixed-Priority (TFP) and Job-Level Fixed-Priority (JFP) scheduling

nodes.name: Two-level EDF via relative priority points
nodes.statement: We consider a task set $\Tbb = \{\tau_1, \dots, \tau_4\}$ of $4$ tasks. In the following we demonstrate how to assign priorities such that $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ are on one priority-level, and $\tau_3$ and $\tau_4$ are on another priority-level, and on each priority-level EDF is utilized. We assign the relative priority points $\Pi_1 = D_1$, $\Pi_2 = D_2$, $\Pi_3 = D_1 + D_2 + D_3$ and $\Pi_4 = D_1 + D_2 + D_4$. If $\Tbb$ is schedulable under EL scheduling with the given relative priority points, then EL produces the same schedule as the desired scheduling policy: Since $\Pi_i - \Pi_j \geq D_i$ for all $i=3,4$ and $j=1,2$, a job $J$ of $\tau_1$ or $\tau_2$ can only have higher priority than a job $J'$ of $\tau_3$ or $\tau_4$ if $J'$ is already finished by the release time of $J$. $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ are scheduled according to EDF, since their relative priority points are set to the deadline. The tasks $\tau_3$ and $\tau_4$ are also scheduled according to EDF, since the difference between the global priorities $\pi_{3,j}$ and $\pi_{4,j'}$ of each two jobs $\tau_{3,j}$ and $\tau_{4,j'}$ is the same as the difference between the absolute deadlines $r_{3,j} + D_3$ and $r_{4,j'} + D_4$.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: Four tasks on two priority levels with EDF in each level, realized by choosing relative priority points.

nodes.name: EL reproduces two-level EDF
nodes.statement: If $\Tbb$ is schedulable under EL scheduling with the given relative priority points, then EL produces the same schedule as the desired scheduling policy:
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
assumptions: $\Tbb$ is schedulable under EL scheduling with the given relative priority points
conclusions: EL produces the same schedule as the desired scheduling policy

nodes.name: Argument for two-level EDF
nodes.statement:
Since $\Pi_i - \Pi_j \geq D_i$ for all $i=3,4$ and $j=1,2$, a job $J$ of $\tau_1$ or $\tau_2$ can only have higher priority than a job $J'$ of $\tau_3$ or $\tau_4$ if $J'$ is already finished by the release time of $J$.
	$\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$ are scheduled according to EDF, since their relative priority points are set to the deadline.
	The tasks $\tau_3$ and $\tau_4$ are also scheduled according to EDF, since the difference between the global priorities $\pi_{3,j}$ and $\pi_{4,j'}$ of each two jobs $\tau_{3,j}$ and $\tau_{4,j'}$ is the same as the difference between the absolute deadlines $r_{3,j} + D_3$ and $r_{4,j'} + D_4$.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: Priority-point gaps separate the levels; within each level priority-point differences equal deadline differences.

nodes.name: Sufficient schedulability test
nodes.statement: In this section, we derive a sufficient schedulability test, i.e., for an arbitrary-deadline task set $\Tbb = \{ \tau_1 , \dots, \tau_n\}$ and an assignment of relative priority points $(\Pi_1, \dots, \Pi_n)$ the test returns \emph{True} if $\Tbb$ is schedulable by the corresponding EL scheduling algorithm.
nodes.section: 4 Schedulability Test for EL Scheduling Algorithms

nodes.name: Active and Current Job
nodes.statement: For a certain schedule, a job $\tau_{k,\ell}$ of a task $\tau_k$ is \emph{active} at time $t$, if it is released but not already finished by time $t$, i.e., $t \in [r_{k,\ell}, f_{k,\ell})$. When there are active jobs of task $\tau_k$ at a time instant $t$, then we call the active job of $\tau_k$ with the earliest release the \emph{current} job of $\tau_k$ at time $t$. We call the task $\tau_k$ active at $t$, if there exists an active job of $\tau_k$ at $t$.
nodes.section: 4 Schedulability Test for EL Scheduling Algorithms
nodes.statement_short: A job is active from release until finish; the current job of a task is its earliest-released active job.

nodes.name: Work, Suspend and Wait
nodes.statement: ~ \begin{itemize} \item The processor is \emph{working on} a job $\tau_{i,j}$ at time $t$, if $\tau_{i,j}$ is executed on the processor at $t$. It is \emph{suspended by} $\tau_{i,j}$ at time $t$, if $\tau_{i,j}$ is suspending itself at $t$, i.e., the remaining suspension time of $\tau_{i,j}$ is reduced. \item We say that the processor is \emph{working} at time $t$ if it is working on any job at $t$. It is \emph{suspended} at $t$, if it is suspended for at least one job but not working on any job at $t$. It is \emph{waiting} at $t$, if it is neither working nor suspended at $t$. The processor is \emph{idle} at $t$, if it is not working at $t$, i.e., if it is suspended or waiting. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 4 Schedulability Test for EL Scheduling Algorithms
nodes.statement_short: Processor states: working on a job, suspended by a job, waiting, idle (suspended or waiting).

nodes.name: Half-open interval convention
nodes.statement: For unambiguous partition of the processor to the different states, we use half-opened intervals, e.g., if the processor is working on a job $\tau_{i,j}$ from time $t_1$ to time $t_2$, then we say that \emph{the processor is working on $\tau_{i,j}$ during $[t_1,t_2)$}.
nodes.section: 4 Schedulability Test for EL Scheduling Algorithms
nodes.definiendum: the processor is working on $\tau_{i,j}$ during $[t_1,t_2)$

nodes.name: Processor States PS 1-3
nodes.statement:
Let $\tau_k \in \Tbb$ be a task. 
	Based on the terminology for different processor states outlined in Section~\ref{sec:system_model}, we distinguish all \textbf{Processor States} (PS) as depicted in Figure~\ref{fig:dec_tree}.
	\begin{itemize}
		\item \textbf{PS~1}: There is no active job of $\tau_k$.
		\item \textbf{PS~2}: There is an active job of $\tau_k$ and the processor is \emph{not} working on a job with higher priority than the current job of task $\tau_k$. 
		\item \textbf{PS~3}: There is an active job of $\tau_k$ and the processor is working on a job with higher priority than the current job of task $\tau_k$.
	\end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: From $\tau_k$'s view: PS 1 no active job; PS 2 active and no higher-priority work; PS 3 active and higher-priority work.

nodes.name: PS 2 means working on or suspended by current job
nodes.statement: In particular, if the processor is in state PS~2, then it is either working on or suspended by the current job of $\tau_k$ since the underlying scheduling algorithm is work-conserving.
assumptions: the processor is in state PS~2
conclusions: it is either working on or suspended by the current job of $\tau_k$

nodes.name: Processor states are exhaustive and exclusive
nodes.statement: At each time, the processor is in exactly one of the above three states.
conclusions: At each time, the processor is in exactly one of the above three states.
nodes.label: lem:processor_states

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8
nodes.statement: This directly follows from the correctness of the decision tree in Figure~\ref{fig:dec_tree}. At each time, the decision tree determines exactly one processor state.
nodes.statement_short: The decision tree assigns exactly one state at each time.

nodes.name: Time in processor states
nodes.statement: Let $[c,d)$ be any half opened interval with $c<d$. \begin{itemize} \item $\widetilde{B}_k(c,d)$ denotes the amount of time during $[c,d)$ where the processor is in state \textbf{PS~1}. \item $B_k(c,d)$ is the amount of time during $[c,d)$ in \textbf{PS~2}. \item For $i \neq k$, $B_k^i(c,d)$ is the amount of time during $[c,d)$ where the processor is in \textbf{PS~3} working on $\tau_i$. More specifically, $\sum_{i\neq k}B_k^i(c,d)$ is the total time during $[c,d)$ in \textbf{PS~3}. \end{itemize} If $c\geq d$, we set all of them, $\widetilde{B}_k(c,d), B_k(c,d), B_k^i(c,d)$, to $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Amounts of time in $[c,d)$ spent in PS 1, PS 2, and PS 3 working on $\tau_i$.
nodes.label: def:B_interferences

nodes.name: Processor state times partition the interval
nodes.statement: For any half opened interval $[c,d)$ with $c<d$ we have \begin{equation} \widetilde{B}_k(c,d) + B_k(c,d) + \sum_{i \neq k} B^i_k(c,d) =(d-c). \end{equation}
also_stated_at: The time in PS~1, PS~2 and PS~3 during some interval $[c,d)$ adds up to the whole interval length.
assumptions: any half opened interval $[c,d)$ with $c<d$
conclusions: \widetilde{B}_k(c,d) + B_k(c,d) + \sum_{i \neq k} B^i_k(c,d) =(d-c).
nodes.label: lem:distribution_ps_with_b

nodes.name: State time decomposition
nodes.statement: \widetilde{B}_k(c,d) + B_k(c,d) + \sum_{i \neq k} B^i_k(c,d) =(d-c).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 10
nodes.statement: This follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:processor_states}.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from Lemma 8.

nodes.name: Job-specific interference terms
nodes.statement: Let $[c,d)$ with $c<d$ be any half opened interval. \begin{itemize} \item $B_{k,\ell}^i(c,d)$ is the amount of time during $[c,d)$ that the processor is working on jobs of $\tau_i$ with higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$. \item $B_{k,\ell}(c,d)$ is the amount of time during $[c,d)$ that the processor is working on or suspended by $\tau_{k,\ell}$ while it is not working on a higher-priority job. \end{itemize} If $c\geq d$, we set all of them to $0$ for simplicity.
nodes.statement_short: Time in $[c,d)$ working on higher-priority jobs of $\tau_i$, and time working on or suspended by $\tau_{k,\ell}$.
nodes.label: def:B_interferences_refinement

nodes.name: PS 2 time as sum over jobs
nodes.statement: For any half opened interval $[c,d)$ we have \begin{equation} B_k(c,d) = \sum_{j \in \Nbb} B_{k,j}(c,d). \end{equation}
assumptions: any half opened interval $[c,d)$
conclusions: B_k(c,d) = \sum_{j \in \Nbb} B_{k,j}(c,d).
nodes.label: lem:refinement_Bk

nodes.name: PS 2 decomposition
nodes.statement: B_k(c,d) = \sum_{j \in \Nbb} B_{k,j}(c,d).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 12
nodes.statement: The lemma follows from the equivalence between: 1)~the processor is in PS~2 and 2)~the processor is \emph{working on or suspended by some job of $\tau_k$ while it is not working on higher-priority jobs}. Since the processor is work-conserving, we obtain an equivalence between 1) and \emph{the processor is working on or suspended by the current job of $\tau_k$ while it is not working on a higher-priority job}. By the definition of the current job, if the processor is working on or suspended by a job, then this is the current job by default. This concludes the equivalence between 1) and 2). By definition, the time of 1) during $[c,d)$ is $B_k(c,d)$, and the time of 2) during $[c,d)$ is $\sum_{j \in \Nbb} B_{k,j}(c,d)$.
nodes.statement_short: Show PS 2 is equivalent to the processor working on or suspended by some job of $\tau_k$ without higher-priority work.

nodes.name: PS 3 time via the last current job
nodes.statement: Consider any half opened interval $[c,d)$. If $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the current job of $\tau_k$ during the whole interval $[c,d)$, then \begin{equation} B^i_k(c,d) = B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d). \end{equation} If $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the current job of $\tau_k$ during $[d-\eps, d)$ for some $\eps >0$, then \begin{equation} B^i_k(c,d) \leq B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d). \end{equation}
assumptions: any half opened interval $[c,d)$
$\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the current job of $\tau_k$ during the whole interval $[c,d)$
$\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the current job of $\tau_k$ during $[d-\eps, d)$ for some $\eps >0$
$\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the current job of $\tau_k$ during the whole interval $[c,d)$
conclusions: B^i_k(c,d) = B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d).

assumptions: $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the current job of $\tau_k$ during $[d-\eps, d)$ for some $\eps >0$
conclusions: B^i_k(c,d) \leq B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d).

nodes.statement_short: PS 3 time equals (or is bounded by) the higher-priority interference w.r.t. the (last) current job $\tau_{k,\ell}$.
conclusions: B^i_k(c,d) = B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d).
B^i_k(c,d) \leq B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d).
nodes.label: lem:refinement_Bik

nodes.name: PS 3 equality
nodes.statement: B^i_k(c,d) = B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d).

nodes.name: PS 3 inequality
nodes.statement: B^i_k(c,d) \leq B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 13
nodes.statement: By definition, $B^i_k(c,d)$ is the amount of time during $[c,d)$ that the processor is working on a job of $\tau_i$ with higher priority than the current job of $\tau_k$. If $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the current job of $\tau_k$ during the whole interval, then $B^i_k(c,d) = B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d)$. If $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is current during $[d-\eps,d)$, then any job of $\tau_k$ which is current at some time during $[c,d)$ has a priority higher than or equal to the priority of $\tau_{k,\ell}$. If the processor is working on a job of $\tau_i$ with higher priority than the current job of $\tau_k$ at that time, then that job of $\tau_i$ has also higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$. As a result, $B^i_k(c,d) \leq B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d)$.
nodes.statement_short: Earlier current jobs have priority at least that of $\tau_{k,\ell}$, so any job beating them also beats $\tau_{k,\ell}$.

nodes.name: Interference terms are non-negative and additive
nodes.statement: By definition, $B_k^i$, $B_k$, $\widetilde{B}_k$, $B_{k,\ell}^i$ and $B_{k,\ell}$ are \emph{non-negative} and \emph{additive}, in the sense that $B(c,d)\geq 0$ and $B(c, d) + B(d,e) = B(c,e)$ for all $B \in \{B_k^i, B_{k}, \widetilde{B}_k, B_{k,\ell}^i, B_{k, \ell}\}$ and $c\leq d \leq e$.
conclusions: $B(c,d)\geq 0$ and $B(c, d) + B(d,e) = B(c,e)$ for all $B \in \{B_k^i, B_{k}, \widetilde{B}_k, B_{k,\ell}^i, B_{k, \ell}\}$ and $c\leq d \leq e$

nodes.name: Enough PS 2 time finishes the job
nodes.statement: If $B_{k,\ell}(c,d) \geq C_k + S_k$, then the job $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is finished by time $d$.
assumptions: $B_{k,\ell}(c,d) \geq C_k + S_k$
conclusions: the job $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is finished by time $d$
nodes.label: lem:Bkl_finished

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 14
nodes.statement: Since $B_{k,\ell}(c,d) \geq C_k + S_k$, the processor is working on the job $\tau_{k,\ell}$ for at least $C_k$ time units during $[c,d)$. As a result, the job finishes no later than at time $d$.
nodes.statement_short: Suspension is at most $S_k$, so at least $C_k$ execution happens in the window.

nodes.name: Non-schedulability condition
nodes.statement: Consider some interval $[c,d)$ with $c\leq d$. If $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is not finished by time d and the task $\tau_k$ is active during (the whole interval) $[c,d)$, then \begin{equation} (C_k+S_k) + \sum_{i \neq k} B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d) + \sum_{j < \ell} B_{k,j}(c,d) > (d-c). \end{equation}
assumptions: some interval $[c,d)$ with $c\leq d$
$\tau_{k,\ell}$ is not finished by time d
the task $\tau_k$ is active during (the whole interval) $[c,d)$
conclusions: (C_k+S_k) + \sum_{i \neq k} B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d) + \sum_{j < \ell} B_{k,j}(c,d) > (d-c).
nodes.statement_short: If $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is unfinished at $d$ while $\tau_k$ stays active, its demand plus interference exceeds $d-c$.
nodes.label: lem:non-sched

nodes.name: Non-schedulability inequality
nodes.statement: (C_k+S_k) + \sum_{i \neq k} B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d) + \sum_{j < \ell} B_{k,j}(c,d) > (d-c).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 15
nodes.statement:
Since $	au_k$ is active during $[c,d)$, we have $\widetilde{B}_k(c,d) = 0$. Using this together with Lemma~ef{lem:distribution_ps_with_b} and Lemma~ef{lem:refinement_Bk} leads to $\sum_{i
eq k} B^i_k(c,d) + \sum_{j\in\Nbb} B_{k,j}(c,d) = (d-c)$. We prove the lemma by showing that  egin{enumerate} \item $\sum_{j \in \Nbb} B_{k,j}(c,d) < C_k+S_k + \sum_{j < \ell} B_{k,j}(c,d)$ and \item $B^i_k(c,d)\leq B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d)$ for all $i
eq k$. \end{enumerate} First, we prove 1). Since $	au_{k,\ell}$ is not finished by time $d$, we know that all $	au_{k,j}$ with $j>\ell$ are not current before $d$. Hence, $B_{k,j}(c,d) = 0$ for all $j > \ell$ and $\sum_{j \in \Nbb} B_{k,j}(c,d) = \sum_{j \leq \ell} B_{k,j}(c,d)$. Moreover, due to Lemma~ef{lem:Bkl_finished}, we have $B_{k,\ell}(c,d) < C_k+S_k$. This proves 1). Second, we prove 2). Since $	au_{k}$ is active during $[c,d)$, by definition, at any time instant $t \in [c, d)$, there is always a job of $	au_k$, which is current. Let the last job of $	au_k$ that is current in this interval be $	au_{k,\ell'}$. That is, there exists some $\eps >0$ such that $	au_{k,\ell'}$ is current during $[d-\eps,d)$. By Lemma~ef{lem:refinement_Bik}, we have $B^i_k(c,d) \leq B^i_{k,\ell'}(c,d)$ for all $i
eq k$. According to the handling mechanism to deal with multiple active jobs of $	au_k$ (for arbitrary-deadline task systems) at the end of Section~ef{sec:system_model}, the jobs of $	au_k$ are executed one after another. Since $	au_{k,\ell'}$ is current in $[d-\eps,d)$, the job $	au_{k,\ell}$ can not have higher priority than $	au_{k, \ell'}$, i.e., $\ell' \leq \ell$ holds. Otherwise, $	au_{k,\ell}$ has to be finished by time $d-\eps$. Therefore, $B^i_{k,\ell'}(c,d) \leq B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d)$ for all $i
eq k$. We conclude that 2) holds.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose $d-c$ via Lemmas 10 and 12, then bound the own-task part (Lemma 14) and the interference part (Lemma 13) separately.

nodes.name: Response-time condition (backbone preparation)
nodes.statement: Let $c\leq d \in \Rbb$ such that either 1) $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is released before $c$, i.e., $c \geq r_{k,\ell}$, or 2)~$c < r_{k,\ell}$ and task $\tau_k$ is active during $[c,r_{k,\ell})$. If \begin{equation} (C_k+ S_k) + \sum_{i \neq k} B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d) + \sum_{j < \ell} B_{k,j}(c,d) \leq (d-c), \end{equation} then $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is finished by time $d$, i.e., $d \geq f_{k,\ell}$.
assumptions: $c\leq d \in \Rbb$ such that either 1) $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is released before $c$, i.e., $c \geq r_{k,\ell}$, or 2)~$c < r_{k,\ell}$ and task $\tau_k$ is active during $[c,r_{k,\ell})$
conclusions: $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is finished by time $d$, i.e., $d \geq f_{k,\ell}$
nodes.statement_short: If demand plus interference in $[c,d)$ is at most $d-c$, the job $\tau_{k,\ell}$ finishes by $d$.
nodes.label: prop:backbone_prep

nodes.name: Backbone condition
nodes.statement: (C_k+ S_k) + \sum_{i \neq k} B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d) + \sum_{j < \ell} B_{k,j}(c,d) \leq (d-c),
nodes.label: eq:prop:backbone_prep

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 16
nodes.statement: We use an indirect proof strategy and assume that $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is not finished by time $d$. In this case, $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is active during $[r_{k,\ell},d)$. Since $r_{k,\ell}\leq c$ or $\tau_k$ is active during $[c,r_{k,\ell})$, we conclude that $\tau_k$ is also active during $[c,d)$. Lemma~\ref{lem:non-sched} states that Equation~\eqref{eq:prop:backbone_prep} does not hold. This contradicts our assumption.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: an unfinished job keeps $\tau_k$ active on $[c,d)$, so Lemma 15 violates the hypothesis.

nodes.name: Analysis Backbone
nodes.statement: Let $c\leq d_{k,\ell} \in \Rbb$ such that either 1)~$\tau_{k,\ell}$ is released before $c$, i.e., $c \geq r_{k,\ell}$ or 2)~$c < r_{k,\ell}$ and task $\tau_k$ is active during $[c,r_{k,\ell})$. If \begin{equation} \widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} \!:=\! (C_k+ S_k) + \!\sum_{i \neq k}\! B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d_{k,\ell}) + \!\sum_{j < \ell}\! B_{k,j}(c,d_{k,\ell}) + c - r_{k,\ell}, \end{equation} is at most $D_k$, then $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ is an upper bound on the response time of $\tau_{k,\ell}$.
assumptions: $c\leq d_{k,\ell} \in \Rbb$ such that either 1)~$\tau_{k,\ell}$ is released before $c$, i.e., $c \geq r_{k,\ell}$ or 2)~$c < r_{k,\ell}$ and task $\tau_k$ is active during $[c,r_{k,\ell})$
conclusions: $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ is an upper bound on the response time of $\tau_{k,\ell}$
nodes.statement_short: Response-time bound $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ from own demand plus interference over $[c,d_{k,\ell})$, valid if at most $D_k$.
nodes.label: cor:backbone

nodes.name: Response time bound R_{k,l}
nodes.statement: \widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} \!:=\! (C_k+ S_k) + \!\sum_{i \neq k}\! B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d_{k,\ell}) + \!\sum_{j < \ell}\! B_{k,j}(c,d_{k,\ell}) + c - r_{k,\ell},
nodes.label: eq:cor_sched_test

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 17
nodes.statement: This corollary follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:backbone_prep} by setting $d:=r_{k,\ell} + \widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$. The case $c>d$ does not occur since otherwise $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} \geq c-r_{k,\ell} > \widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ would hold by definition of $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ and $d$. We only consider $c \leq d$. Since $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} \leq D_k$ by assumption, we have $d\leq d_{k,\ell}$. Hence, $B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d)\leq B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d_{k,\ell})$ and $B_{k,j}(c,d) \leq B_{k,j}(c,d_{k,\ell})$ for all $i$ and all $j$. As a result, the left hand side of Equation~\eqref{eq:prop:backbone_prep} is less than or equal to $(C_k+ S_k) + \sum_{i \neq k} B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d_{k,\ell}) + \sum_{j < \ell} B_{k,j}(c,d_{k,\ell})$, which is the same as $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} + r_{k,\ell} - c = d-c$ by definition. Since all assumptions from Proposition~\ref{prop:backbone_prep} hold, the job $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is finished by time $d=\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} + r_{k,\ell}$. Hence, $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ is an upper bound on the response time of $\tau_{k,\ell}$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 16 with $d:=r_{k,\ell}+\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$, using monotonicity of the $B$ terms in the window end.

nodes.name: Higher-priority jobs meet their deadlines
nodes.statement: We do this under the assumption that all jobs with higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$ meet their deadline, since this is our induction hypothesis later used in Theorem~\ref{thm:suff_sched_test_fixed} and Lemma~\ref{lem:suff_sched_test_var_prep}.

nodes.name: Response time upper bounds of other tasks
nodes.statement:
For each task $\tau_i \neq \tau_k$ let $\widetilde{R}_i$ be an upper bound on the worst-case response time (WCRT) of jobs of $\tau_i$ with higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$.
	If there is no upper bound available yet, we set $\widetilde{R}_i := D_i$, as all jobs with higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$ meet their deadline.

nodes.name: Number of higher-priority jobs of the same task
nodes.statement: The number of jobs of $\tau_k$ with higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$ which can be executed during $[c,d_{k,\ell})$ is upper bounded by $\ceiling{\frac{d_{k,\ell}-c}{T_k}}-1$.
conclusions: The number of jobs of $\tau_k$ with higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$ which can be executed during $[c,d_{k,\ell})$ is upper bounded by $\ceiling{\frac{d_{k,\ell}-c}{T_k}}-1$
nodes.label: lem:number_active_jobs

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 18
nodes.statement: The formula $\ceiling{\frac{d_{k,\ell}-c}{T_k}}$ counts the maximal number of deadlines of $\tau_k$ in $(c,d_{k,\ell}]$. Since $\tau_{k,\ell}$ has deadline at the end of the analysis window but it has no higher priority than itself, we remove one job.
nodes.statement_short: Count deadlines of $\tau_k$ in $(c,d_{k,\ell}]$ and remove $\tau_{k,\ell}$ itself.

nodes.name: Bound B1
nodes.statement: The total amount of time that the processor is working on or suspended by higher-priority jobs of $\tau_k$ while not working on higher priority jobs of other tasks is upper bounded by \begin{equation} \sum_{j < \ell} B_{k,j}(c,d_{k,\ell}) \leq \left(\ceiling{\frac{d_{k,\ell}-c}{T_k}}-1\right) \cdot (C_k+S_k). \end{equation}
conclusions: \sum_{j < \ell} B_{k,j}(c,d_{k,\ell}) \leq \left(\ceiling{\frac{d_{k,\ell}-c}{T_k}}-1\right) \cdot (C_k+S_k).
nodes.statement_short: Self-interference from earlier jobs of $\tau_k$ is at most (number of such jobs) times $C_k+S_k$.
nodes.label: lem:upper_bound_sum_Bkj

nodes.name: Bound B1 inequality
nodes.statement: \sum_{j < \ell} B_{k,j}(c,d_{k,\ell}) \leq \left(\ceiling{\frac{d_{k,\ell}-c}{T_k}}-1\right) \cdot (C_k+S_k).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 19
nodes.statement: This follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:number_active_jobs} and the upper bounds $C_k$ for execution and $S_k$ for suspension.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply the job count of Lemma 18 by $C_k+S_k$.

nodes.name: Interference job count via priority points
nodes.statement: There are at most $\max\left(\ceiling{\frac{\Pi_k-\Pi_i+\widetilde{R}_i+r_{k,\ell}-c}{T_i}}, 0\right)$ jobs of $\tau_i,~i\neq k$ with higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$ that are executed during the interval $[c, d_{k,\ell})$.
conclusions: There are at most $\max\left(\ceiling{\frac{\Pi_k-\Pi_i+\widetilde{R}_i+r_{k,\ell}-c}{T_i}}, 0\right)$ jobs of $\tau_i,~i\neq k$ with higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$ that are executed during the interval $[c, d_{k,\ell})$
nodes.statement_short: Counts higher-priority jobs of $\tau_i$ released between $c-\widetilde{R}_i$ and $r_{k,\ell}+\Pi_k-\Pi_i$.
nodes.label: lem:ineqk_1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 20
nodes.statement: A job of $\tau_i$ can only be executed during $[c,d_{k,\ell})$, if it is released after $c-\widetilde{R}_i$. Moreover, it can have higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$, if it is released no later than $r_{k,\ell} + \Pi_k - \Pi_i$. We count the maximal number of releases of $\tau_i$ during $(c-\widetilde{R}_i, r_{k,\ell} + \Pi_k - \Pi_i)$ by $\ceiling{\frac{r_{k,\ell} + \Pi_k - \Pi_i - c + \widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}}$ if the interval has non-negative length. Otherwise, the number of releases is $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Count releases of $\tau_i$ in the window of jobs that can both run after $c$ and have higher priority.

nodes.name: Argument for interference bound via priority points
nodes.statement: The processor is working on each job of $\tau_i$ for at most $C_i$ time units.
nodes.statement_short: Each job of $\tau_i$ executes at most $C_i$; combine with the job count of Lemma 20.

nodes.name: Interference bound via priority points
nodes.statement: Hence, we have an upper bound of $B_{k,\ell}^i(c,d_{k,\ell}) \leq \max\left(\ceiling{\frac{\Pi_k-\Pi_i+\widetilde{R}_i+r_{k,\ell}-c}{T_i}}, 0\right) \cdot C_i$.
conclusions: $B_{k,\ell}^i(c,d_{k,\ell}) \leq \max\left(\ceiling{\frac{\Pi_k-\Pi_i+\widetilde{R}_i+r_{k,\ell}-c}{T_i}}, 0\right) \cdot C_i$

nodes.name: Looseness of the priority-point bound
nodes.statement:
In the above proof we only compare if the job can work \emph{after} $c$.
	We do not check if the job can work \emph{before} $d_{k,\ell}$.
	As a result, the estimation can become very loose if $\Pi_k$ is very high compared to $\Pi_i$, e.g., when applying the schedulability test to TFP scheduling.
	Therefore, we combine the estimation with a second approach.
nodes.statement_short: The bound ignores whether a job can run before $d_{k,\ell}$, so it is loose when $\Pi_k\gg\Pi_i$ (e.g. TFP).

nodes.name: Interference bound via deadline
nodes.statement: For $i\neq k$, $B_{k,\ell}^i(c,d_{k,\ell})$ is upper bounded by $\max\left\{\ceiling{\frac{D_k-C_i+r_{k,\ell}-c+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}}C_i, 0\right\}$.
assumptions: $i\neq k$
conclusions: $B_{k,\ell}^i(c,d_{k,\ell})$ is upper bounded by $\max\left\{\ceiling{\frac{D_k-C_i+r_{k,\ell}-c+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}}C_i, 0\right\}$
nodes.label: lem:ineqk_2

nodes.name: Intuition for Lemma 21
nodes.statement:
Intuitively, the maximal interference from task $\tau_i$ is obtained when the \emph{last} interfering job of $\tau_i$ is released at $d_{k,\ell}-C_i$ and executed for $C_i$ time units during $[d_{k,\ell}-C_i, d_{k,\ell})$.
	The maximum interference is then calculated by the number of releases during $(c-\widetilde{R}_i, d_{k,\ell}-C_i]$ multiplied with $C_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Worst case: the last interfering job is released at $d_{k,\ell}-C_i$; count releases in $(c-\widetilde{R}_i, d_{k,\ell}-C_i]$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 21
nodes.statement: If there is no job of $\tau_i$ executed during $[c,d_{k,\ell})$, then $B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d_{k,\ell})=0$ and the lemma is proven. Otherwise, let $\tau_{i,j'}$ be the last job of $\tau_i$ being executed during $[c,d_{k,\ell})$. We isolate that job in the following way. Let $r_{i,j'}$ be the release time of $\tau_{i,j'}$ and let $C^*$ be the amount of time that the processor is working on $\tau_{i,j'}$ during the interval $[c,d_{k,\ell})$. We have $B(c,d_{k,\ell}) \leq B(c,r_{i,j'}) + C^*.$ If $r_{i,j'}-c < (C-C^*)$, then $B(c,r_{i,j'}) + C^* \leq C$. Moreover, $\ceiling{\frac{D_k-C_i+r_{k,\ell}-c+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}}C_i \geq \ceiling{\frac{D_k+r_{k,\ell}-c}{T_i}}C_i \geq C_i$ since there is a job being executed during $[c, d_{k,\ell})$, i.e., $c < D_k+r_{k,\ell}$. In this case the lemma is proven. If $r_{i,j'}-c \geq (C-C^*)$, then $B(c,r_{i,j'}) + C^* \leq B(c + (C_i-C^*),r_{i,j'}) + C_i$, i.e., we over approximate be replacing $(C_i-C^*)$ time units at the beginning by execution time. Next we compute $B(c + (C_i-C^*),r_{i,j'})$ by counting the number of releases during the interval $(c+(C_i-C^*)-\widetilde{R}_i, r_{i,j'}-T_i]$. It is $ \ceiling{\frac{r_{i,j'}-T_i-c-C_i+C*+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}} \leq \ceiling{\frac{r_{k,\ell}-T_i-c-C_i+D_k+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}} = \ceiling{\frac{r_{k,\ell}-c-C_i+D_k+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}} -1 $ where we use that $r_{i,j'} + C^* \leq r_{k,\ell} + D_k$. In total, the value of $B(c,d_{k,\ell})$ is then upper bounded by $\ceiling{\frac{r_{k,\ell}-c-C_i+D_k+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}} \cdot C_i$ in this case.
nodes.statement_short: Isolate the last interfering job of $\tau_i$; in two cases bound the interference before its release by counting releases.

nodes.name: Bound B2
nodes.statement: For $i\neq k$ the value of $B_{k,\ell}^i(c,d_{k,\ell})$ is upper bounded by \begin{equation} B_{k,\ell}^i (c,d_{k,\ell}) \leq \max\left(\ceiling{\frac{G_{k}^i+\widetilde{R}_i+r_{k,\ell}-c}{T_i}}, 0\right)C_i \end{equation} where $G_k^i:= \min(D_k-C_i, \Pi_k-\Pi_i)$.
assumptions: $i\neq k$
$G_k^i:= \min(D_k-C_i, \Pi_k-\Pi_i)$
conclusions:
B_{k,\ell}^i (c,d_{k,\ell}) \leq
				\max\left(\ceiling{\frac{G_{k}^i+\widetilde{R}_i+r_{k,\ell}-c}{T_i}}, 0\right)C_i
nodes.statement_short: Interference from $\tau_i$ bounded using $G_k^i=\min(D_k-C_i,\Pi_k-\Pi_i)$, combining Lemmas 20 and 21.
nodes.label: lem:total_bound_interference

nodes.name: Bound B2 inequality
nodes.statement: B_{k,\ell}^i (c,d_{k,\ell}) \leq \max\left(\ceiling{\frac{G_{k}^i+\widetilde{R}_i+r_{k,\ell}-c}{T_i}}, 0\right)C_i
nodes.label: eq:total_bound_interference

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 22
nodes.statement: This is a combination of the results from Lemma~\ref{lem:ineqk_1} and Lemma~\ref{lem:ineqk_2}.
nodes.statement_short: Take the minimum of the bounds from Lemmas 20 and 21.

nodes.name: Schedulability test with fixed analysis window
nodes.statement: \small \caption{Schedulability test with fixed analysis window.} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \item[] \textbf{Input:} $\Tbb = \{\tau_1,\dots,\tau_n\}$, $(\Pi_1,\dots,\Pi_n)$, $\eta$, $depth$ \item[] \textbf{Output:} True: schedulable, False: no decision \item[] \State Order $\tau_1 ,\dots,\tau_n$, s.th. $D_1\geq \dots \geq D_n$. \State Set $\widetilde{R}_i := D_i$ for all $i$. \For{$i=1, 2, \dots, depth$} \State $solved := True$ \For{$k = 1, 2, \dots,n$} \State $cand := [~]$; $step := \eta \cdot {D_k}$ \Comment{Preparation.} \For{$b = 0, step, 2\cdot step, \cdots < D_k$} \Comment{Compute.} \State $cand.append(\widetilde{R}_k(b))$ using Equation~\eqref{eq:suff_sched_test_fixed}. \EndFor \State $\widetilde{R}_k := \min\limits (cand)$ \Comment{Compare candidates.} \If{$\widetilde{R}_k>D_k$} \Comment{Check condition.} \State $solved := False$; $\widetilde{R}_k := D_k$; \textbf{break} \EndIf \EndFor \EndFor \State \Return $solved$ \end{algorithmic}
nodes.statement_short: Iteratively refine response-time bounds $\widetilde{R}_k$ by a grid search over $b$ of Theorem 23's bound; fail if any exceeds $D_k$.
nodes.label: alg:sched_test_fixed

nodes.name: Fixed analysis window
nodes.statement: In this section, we fix the analysis window, i.e., the possible range of $c$ from the previous sections, to the interval $[r_{k,\ell}, d_{k,\ell})$.

nodes.name: Sufficient Schedulability Test (fixed analysis window)
nodes.statement: Let $\Tbb = \{\tau_1,\dots.\tau_n\}$ be an arbitrary-deadline task set with relative priority points $(\Pi_1, \dots, \Pi_n)$. If for all $k=1, \dots, n$ there exists some $b_k \in [0,D_k)$ such that \begin{equation} \widetilde{R}_k(b_k) \leq D_k, \end{equation} where $\widetilde{R}_k(b_k):=\ceiling{\frac{D_k-b_k}{T_k}}(C_k + S_k) + b_k + \sum\limits_{i\neq k} \max\left(\ceiling{\frac{G_k^i+ \widetilde{R}_i-b_k}{T_i}}, 0\right) C_i$ and $G^i_k = \min(D_k-C_i, \Pi_k-\Pi_i)$, then the task set is schedulable by EL scheduling with the given relative priority points and the worst-case response time of $\tau_k$ is upper bounded by $\widetilde{R}_k := \widetilde{R}_k(b_k)$.
assumptions: $\Tbb = \{\tau_1,\dots.\tau_n\}$ be an arbitrary-deadline task set with relative priority points $(\Pi_1, \dots, \Pi_n)$
for all $k=1, \dots, n$ there exists some $b_k \in [0,D_k)$ such that
conclusions: the task set is schedulable by EL scheduling with the given relative priority points and the worst-case response time of $\tau_k$ is upper bounded by $\widetilde{R}_k := \widetilde{R}_k(b_k)$
nodes.statement_short: If for each task some offset $b_k$ makes the TDA-like bound $\widetilde{R}_k(b_k)\le D_k$, the set is EL-schedulable with WCRT $\widetilde{R}_k(b_k)$.
nodes.label: thm:suff_sched_test_fixed

nodes.name: Fixed-window test condition
nodes.statement: \widetilde{R}_k(b_k) \leq D_k,
nodes.label: eq:suff_sched_test_fixed

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 23
nodes.statement: Assume we have found $b_k,~k=1,\dots,n$ such that Equation~\eqref{eq:suff_sched_test_fixed} holds. We consider some schedule obtained by this task set and denote by $Seq$ the sequence of all jobs in the schedule ordered by their priority. Via induction, we prove that the first $\xi$ jobs in $Seq$ have the required response time upper bound, for all $\xi \in \Nbb_0$. Consequently, $\widetilde{R}_k$ is an upper bound on the worst-case response time of $\tau_k$ for all $k$ and the task set is schedulable. \textbf{Initial case:} $\xi = 0$. In this case, the set of the first $\xi$ jobs in $Seq$ is $\{\}$ the empty set. Trivially, all of them have the required response time upper bound. \textbf{Induction step:} $\xi \to \xi+1$. By assumption, the first $\xi$ jobs in $Seq$ have the required response time upper bound. We denote the $(\xi+1)$-th job in $Seq$ by $\tau_{k,\ell}$. We aim to use Corollary~\ref{cor:backbone} to prove that the response time of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is upper bounded by $\widetilde{R}_k$. By definition, we have $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} = (C_k+ S_k) + \sum_{i \neq k} B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d_{k,\ell}) + \sum_{j < \ell} B_{k,j}(c,d_{k,\ell}) + c - r_{k,\ell}$. Since all higher priority jobs have the required response time upper bound, we can use the estimation from Section~\ref{sec:estimation_B}. Using Lemma~\ref{lem:upper_bound_sum_Bkj} and Lemma~\ref{lem:total_bound_interference}, we obtain $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} \leq \widetilde{R}_k$ when choosing $c:= b_k+r_{k,\ell}$. Due to Equation~\eqref{eq:suff_sched_test_fixed}, even $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} \leq \widetilde{R}_k \leq D_k$. We use Corollary~\ref{cor:backbone} to conclude that $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ is an upper bound on the response time of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ and therefore $\widetilde{R}_k$ is an upper bound on the response time of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: Induction over jobs in priority order. The step applies the Analysis Backbone with $c:=b_k+r_{k,\ell}$ and Bounds B1, B2.

nodes.name: Relation to TDA and implementation challenges
nodes.statement_short: The test resembles TDA but needs good choices of $b_k$ and handling of mutually dependent $\widetilde{R}_k$.

nodes.name: Step size parameter eta
nodes.statement: For $b_k$, we discretize the search space into $\frac{1}{\eta}$ values with a step size $\eta \cdot D_k$, for a user-specified parameter $\eta$.

nodes.name: Time complexity of Algorithm 1
nodes.statement: The time complexity of Algorithm~\ref{alg:sched_test_fixed} is $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{depth\cdot n^2}{\eta}\right)$.
conclusions: The time complexity of Algorithm~\ref{alg:sched_test_fixed} is $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{depth\cdot n^2}{\eta}\right)$

nodes.name: Computed values are upper bounds
nodes.statement:
Please note that the computed values of $\widetilde{R}_k$ are in fact only upper bounds of $\widetilde{R}_k$ from Theorem~\ref{thm:suff_sched_test_fixed}.
	A reduction of $\widetilde{R}_i,~i\neq k$ in subsequent iterations reduces the actual value of $\widetilde{R}_k$ as well, since $\widetilde{R}_k$ is monotonically increasing with respect to $\widetilde{R}_i,$ for all $i\neq k$.
nodes.statement_short: Algorithm 1's values over-approximate Theorem 23's $\widetilde{R}_k$, which is monotone in the other $\widetilde{R}_i$.

nodes.name: Variable analysis window
nodes.statement: For the schedulability test with variable analysis window, we gradually increase the length of the active interval, i.e., $a = 0,1,2,\dots$ and analyze the window $[c,d_{k,\ell})$ with $c \in [r_{k,\ell-a}, d_{k,\ell})$.

nodes.name: Variable and fixed windows coincide for constrained deadlines
nodes.statement:
Please note that this approach only differs from the case with fixed analysis window when considering arbitrary deadline tasks.
	For constrained deadline task sets, the variable analysis window approach coincides with the fixed analysis window approach, as the algorithm stops at $a=0$ without enlarging the analysis window.
assumptions: constrained deadline task sets
conclusions: the variable analysis window approach coincides with the fixed analysis window approach

nodes.name: Active interval
nodes.statement: Let $a\in \Nbb_0$. A job $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the $(a+1)$-th job in an \emph{active interval} of $\tau_k$, if the following two conditions hold. \begin{itemize} \item $\tau_k$ is active during $[r_{k,\ell-a},f_{k,\ell})$. \item At time $r_{k,\ell-a}$ there is no active job which is released \emph{before} $r_{k,\ell-a}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the $(a+1)$-th job of an active interval if $\tau_k$ is busy from $r_{k,\ell-a}$ with no earlier backlog.
nodes.label: def:active_int

nodes.name: Only jobs of the active interval are current
nodes.statement:
If $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the $(a+1)$-th job in an active interval of $\tau_k$, then only $\tau_{k,\ell-a}, \dots, \tau_{k,\ell}$ are current jobs of $\tau_k$ during $[r_{k,\ell-a},f_{k,\ell})$.
	More specifically, in this case the value of $B_{k,j}(c,d_{k,\ell})$ is $0$ if $c \geq r_{k,\ell-a}$ and $j<\ell-a$.
assumptions: $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the $(a+1)$-th job in an active interval of $\tau_k$
conclusions: only $\tau_{k,\ell-a}, \dots, \tau_{k,\ell}$ are current jobs of $\tau_k$ during $[r_{k,\ell-a},f_{k,\ell})$
the value of $B_{k,j}(c,d_{k,\ell})$ is $0$ if $c \geq r_{k,\ell-a}$ and $j<\ell-a$

nodes.name: Response time bound with variable window
nodes.statement: Let $\tau_{k,\ell}$ be the $(a+1)$-th job in an active interval of $\tau_k$ and let all higher-priority jobs meet their deadline. Let $\widetilde{R}_i,~i\neq k$ be an upper bound on the response time of all higher-priority jobs of $\tau_i$. If there exists some $c \in [r_{k,\ell-a},d_{k,\ell})$ such that \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &\min \left( a+1, \ceiling{\frac{d_{k,\ell}-c}{T_k}} \right) (C_k+S_k) \\&+ \sum_{i \neq k} \max\left( \ceiling{\frac{G^i_k+\widetilde{R}_i+r_{k,\ell}-c}{T_i}}, 0 \right) C_i + c - r_{k,\ell} \end{aligned} \end{equation} is at most $D_k$, with $G^i_k := \min(D_k-C_i, \Pi_k-\Pi_i)$, then \eqref{eq:lem_var_window} is an upper bound on the response time of $\tau_{k,\ell}$.
assumptions: $\tau_{k,\ell}$ be the $(a+1)$-th job in an active interval of $\tau_k$
all higher-priority jobs meet their deadline
$\widetilde{R}_i,~i\neq k$ be an upper bound on the response time of all higher-priority jobs of $\tau_i$
there exists some $c \in [r_{k,\ell-a},d_{k,\ell})$ such that
conclusions: \eqref{eq:lem_var_window} is an upper bound on the response time of $\tau_{k,\ell}$
nodes.statement_short: Within an active interval only $a$ earlier own jobs interfere, giving a tighter response-time bound.
nodes.label: lem:suff_sched_test_var_prep

nodes.name: Variable-window response bound
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} &\min \left( a+1, \ceiling{\frac{d_{k,\ell}-c}{T_k}} \right) (C_k+S_k) \\&+ \sum_{i \neq k} \max\left( \ceiling{\frac{G^i_k+\widetilde{R}_i+r_{k,\ell}-c}{T_i}}, 0 \right) C_i + c - r_{k,\ell} \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:lem_var_window

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 25
nodes.statement: For the proof, we apply Corollary~\ref{cor:backbone}. Since $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the $(a+1)$-th job in an active interval, $\tau_k$ is active during $[r_{k,\ell-a}, r_{k,\ell})$. Hence, the restriction on $c$ in Corollary~\ref{cor:backbone} are fulfilled by default, when $c$ is chosen from $[r_{k,\ell-a}, d_{k,\ell})$. Moreover, since $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the $(a+1)$-th job in an active interval, the jobs $\tau_{k,1}, \dots, \tau_{k,\ell-a-1}$ are finished by time $r_{k,\ell-a}$. We obtain $\sum_{j < \ell-a} B_{k,j} (c,d_{k,\ell}) \leq \sum_{j < \ell-a} B_{k,j} (r_{k,\ell-a},d_{k,\ell}) = 0$. Hence, $ \sum_{j < \ell} B_{k,j} (c,d_{k,\ell}) = \sum_{j = \ell-a}^{\ell-1} B_{k,j} (c,d_{k,\ell}) \leq \sum_{j = \ell-a}^{\ell-1} (C_k+S_k) = a\cdot (C_k+S_k). $ We combine this with the results from Lemma~\ref{lem:upper_bound_sum_Bkj} and Lemma~\ref{lem:total_bound_interference}, and obtain that $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ from Equation~\eqref{eq:cor_sched_test} is less than or equal to the value in Equation~\eqref{eq:lem_var_window}. If \eqref{eq:lem_var_window} is at most $D_k$, then $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}\leq D_k$. Corollary~\ref{cor:backbone} states that $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ is an upper bound on the response time of $r_{k,\ell}$ and therefore, also \eqref{eq:lem_var_window} is an upper bound on the response time.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Analysis Backbone; jobs before the active interval contribute nothing, earlier own jobs at most $a(C_k+S_k)$.

nodes.name: Sufficient Schedulability Test (variable analysis window)
nodes.statement: Let $\Tbb=\{\tau_1, \dots, \tau_n\}$ be an arbitrary-deadline task set with relative priority points $(\Pi_1, \dots, \Pi_n)$. We define the function $\widetilde{R}^a_k : \Rbb_{\geq 0} \to \Rbb_{\geq 0}$ by the assignment \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} x \mapsto &\min\left(a+1, \ceiling{\frac{D_k-x+aT_k}{T_k}}\right)(C_k+S_k) \\&+ \sum_{i \neq k} \max \left( \ceiling{\frac{G^k_i + \widetilde{R}_i-x+aT_k}{T_i}},0 \right) C_i + x-aT_k. \end{aligned} \end{equation} If for all $k=1,\dots,n$ there exists $\tilde a_k \in \Nbb_0$, such that for all $a = 0,\dots,\tilde a_k$ there exists $b^a_k \in [0,a T_k + D_k)$, such that \begin{equation} \widetilde{R}^a_k(b^a_k) \leq D_k, \text{ and furthermore } \widetilde{R}^{\tilde a_k}_k(b^{\tilde a_k}_k) \leq T_k, \end{equation} then the task set is schedulable by EL scheduling with the given relative priority points and $\widetilde{R}_k := \max_{a = 0, \dots, \tilde a} \widetilde{R}^a_k(b^a_k)$ is an upper bound on the WCRT of $\tau_k$ for all $k$.
assumptions: $\Tbb=\{\tau_1, \dots, \tau_n\}$ be an arbitrary-deadline task set with relative priority points $(\Pi_1, \dots, \Pi_n)$
conclusions: the task set is schedulable by EL scheduling with the given relative priority points and $\widetilde{R}_k := \max_{a = 0, \dots, \tilde a} \widetilde{R}^a_k(b^a_k)$ is an upper bound on the WCRT of $\tau_k$ for all $k$
nodes.statement_short: If for each task the active-interval bounds $\widetilde{R}^a_k$ stay below $D_k$ up to an $\tilde a_k$ where they drop below $T_k$, the set is EL-schedulable.
nodes.label: thm:suff_sched_test_var

nodes.name: Variable-window bound function
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} x \mapsto &\min\left(a+1, \ceiling{\frac{D_k-x+aT_k}{T_k}}\right)(C_k+S_k) \\&+ \sum_{i \neq k} \max \left( \ceiling{\frac{G^k_i + \widetilde{R}_i-x+aT_k}{T_i}},0 \right) C_i + x-aT_k. \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:thm:suff_sched_test_var

nodes.name: Variable-window test conditions
nodes.statement: \widetilde{R}^a_k(b^a_k) \leq D_k, \text{ and furthermore } \widetilde{R}^{\tilde a_k}_k(b^{\tilde a_k}_k) \leq T_k,

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 26
nodes.statement: The proof is similar to the one of Theorem~\ref{thm:suff_sched_test_fixed}. Let $Seq$ be the sequence of all jobs in the schedule ordered by their priority. By induction we show that the following response time upper bound holds for the first $\xi \in \Nbb_0$ jobs in $Seq$: \begin{enumerate} \item $\widetilde{R}_k$ for all jobs of $\tau_k$ for each task $\tau_k$. \item $T_k$ for all $\tilde a_k$-th jobs in an active interval of $\tau_k$ for each task $\tau_k$. \end{enumerate} \textbf{Initial case:} $\xi_0$. The initial case is again trivially fulfilled, since there has nothing to be checked when there are no jobs. \textbf{Induction step:} $\xi \to \xi+1$. The first $\xi$ jobs in $Seq$ have the required response time upper bounds 1) and 2) by induction. We denote by $\tau_{k,\ell}$ the $(\xi+1)$-th job of $Seq$. Let $a$ be the lowest value in $\Nbb_0$, such that $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the $(a+1)$-th job in an active interval of $\tau_k$. We first show that $a\leq \tilde a_k$ by contraposition. If $a > \tilde a$, then we consider the job $\tau_{k,\ell-(a-\tilde a)}$. This is the $(\tilde a+1)$-th job in an active interval of $\tau_k$. Moreover, this job is one of the first $\xi$ jobs in $Seq$ and therefore has a response time of at most $T_k$ due to 2). Hence, $\tau_{k,\ell-(a-\tilde a)}$ is finished by time $r_{k,\ell-(a-\tilde a)+1}$. We conclude that $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the $(a-\tilde a_k)$-th job in an active interval of $\tau_k$, which contradicts the minimality of $a$. We now choose $c:=b^a_k-a\cdot T_k + r_{k,\ell}$. Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:suff_sched_test_var_prep} with this $c$ shows that $\widetilde{R}^a_k(b^a_k)$ is a response time upper bound of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Induction over jobs in priority order as for Theorem 23. The step bounds the active-interval index by $\tilde a_k$ and applies Lemma 25.

nodes.name: Parameter max_a
nodes.statement: To make the schedulability test deterministic, we introduce an additional parameter $max\_a$ which aborts the loop when even $a=max\_a$ gives no result.

nodes.name: Schedulability test with variable analysis window
nodes.statement: \small \caption{Schedulability test with var.\@ analysis window.} \begin{algorithmic}[1] \item[] \textbf{Input:} $\Tbb = \{\tau_1,\dots,\tau_n\}$, $(\Pi_1,\dots,\Pi_n)$, $\eta$, $max\_a$, $depth$ \item[] \textbf{Output:} True: schedulable, False: no decision \item[] \State Order $\tau_1 ,\dots,\tau_n$, s.th. $D_1\geq \dots \geq D_n$. \State Set $\widetilde{R}_i := D_i$ for all $i$. \For{$i=1,2, \dots, depth$} \State $solved := True$ \For{$k = 1, 2, \dots,n$} \For{$a=0,1, \dots, max\_a$} \Comment{Different $a$.} \State $cand := [~]$; $step := \eta \cdot D_k$ \Comment{Preparation.} \For{$b=0,step, 2\cdot step, \dots <aT_k + D_k$} \State $\triangleright$ Compute candidate: \State $cand.append(\widetilde{R}^a_k(b))$ from Equation~\eqref{eq:thm:suff_sched_test_var} \EndFor \State $\widetilde{R}^a_k := \min\limits (cand)$ \Comment{Compare candidates.} \If{$\widetilde{R}^a_k\leq T_k$}\Comment{Check~cond.~1.} \State $\triangleright$ WCRT upper bound: \State $\tilde{a} := a$; $\widetilde{R}_k := \min_{a=0,\dots,\tilde a} \widetilde{R}^a_k$; \textbf{break} \EndIf \If{$\widetilde{R}^a_k>D_k$ or $a=max\_a$} \Comment{Check cond.~2.} \State $solved:=False$; $\widetilde{R}_k := D_k$; \textbf{break} \EndIf \EndFor \EndFor \EndFor \State \Return $solved$ \end{algorithmic}
