nodes.statement_short: Like Algorithm 1 but loops over active-interval length $a$ until $\widetilde{R}^a_k\le T_k$, aborting at $max\_a$ or when exceeding $D_k$.
nodes.label: alg:sched_test_var

nodes.name: Variable window bound lower bounded by fixed window bound
nodes.statement: When setting $x = b_k + a\cdot T_k$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:suff_sched_test_var}, then the result is lower bounded by $\widetilde{R}_k(b_k)$ from Theorem~\ref{thm:suff_sched_test_fixed}.
nodes.section: 4.5 Dominance of Fixed and Variable Analysis Window
assumptions: setting $x = b_k + a\cdot T_k$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:suff_sched_test_var}
conclusions: the result is lower bounded by $\widetilde{R}_k(b_k)$ from Theorem~\ref{thm:suff_sched_test_fixed}

nodes.name: Fixed and variable windows do not dominate each other
nodes.statement: However, both methods do not dominate each other, as demonstrated in the discussion of Figure~\ref{fig:eval_arbdl_dm} in Section~\ref{sec:evaluation}, due to the following reasons.
nodes.section: 4.5 Dominance of Fixed and Variable Analysis Window
conclusions: both methods do not dominate each other

nodes.name: Reasons for non-dominance
nodes.statement:
First, the analysis with variable analysis window can only analyze schedules where the length of active intervals is bounded.
More specifically, if the response-time upper bound $\widetilde{R}^a_k$ is in the interval $(T_k, D_k)$ for all $a$, then the schedulability test with the variable analysis window never deems the task schedulable.
Second, by setting $max\_a$ this effect is even intensified:
The analysis with variable analysis window has to find $\widetilde{R}^a_k \leq T_k$ even for some $a \leq max\_a$.
Third, the discretization using $\eta$ in Algorithm~\ref{alg:sched_test_fixed} and~\ref{alg:sched_test_var} ensures the same number of points for each analysis interval.
As a result, not all points $b+aT_k$ with $b$ from Algorithm~\ref{alg:sched_test_fixed} are checked during Algorithm~\ref{alg:sched_test_var} as well.
nodes.section: 4.5 Dominance of Fixed and Variable Analysis Window
nodes.statement_short: Three reasons: the variable window needs bounded active intervals, $max\_a$ restricts it further, and $\eta$-discretization checks different points.

nodes.name: EDF mechanism workflow
nodes.statement_short: Generic EDF dispatcher: map release to priority, insert into ordered ready queue, run highest-priority job.

nodes.name: Every EDF-capable RTOS can realize EL scheduling
nodes.statement:
Since the realization on both RTOSes only requires slight modifications,
	we conjecture that every RTOS supporting EDF scheduling can also realize EL scheduling.
assumptions: RTOS supporting EDF scheduling
conclusions: every RTOS supporting EDF scheduling can also realize EL scheduling

nodes.name: Acceptance ratio
nodes.statement: In each figure, we present the \emph{acceptance ratio} which is the share of task sets that are deemed schedulable by the schedulability test under consideration.

nodes.name: Synthetic task set generation
nodes.statement:
For the experiments, we synthesize $500$ task sets for each utilization from $0\%$ to $100\%$ in steps of $5\%$.
	For each task set we generate $50$ tasks.
	We first generate $50$ utilization values $U_i$ using the UUniFast~\cite{DBLP:journals/rts/BiniB05} method with the given total utilization goal, and then adopt the suggestion by Emberson~et~al.~\cite{emberson2010techniques} to pull the minimum inter-arrival time $T_i$ according to a log-uniform distribution from the interval $[1,100] [ms]$.
	The worst-case execution time is computed by $C_i = T_i \cdot U_i$ and the deadline is set to the minimum inter-arrival time $D_i = T_i$.
	For each task, we draw the maximum suspension time $S_i$ uniformly at random from $[0,0.5(T_i-C_i)]$.
nodes.statement_short: Generate 50-task sets: UUniFast utilizations, log-uniform periods, $C_i=T_iU_i$, $D_i=T_i$, uniform suspensions.

nodes.name: EL DM performs similar to state of the art
nodes.statement: As depicted, our schedulability test performs similar to the state-of-the-art methods.
conclusions: our schedulability test performs similar to the state-of-the-art methods

nodes.name: EL EDF improves the state of the art
nodes.statement: \textbf{EL EDF} improves the state of the art.
conclusions: \textbf{EL EDF} improves the state of the art

nodes.name: Best lambda improves EQDF and SAEDF
nodes.statement: As depicted, choosing $\lambda$ to be the best integer in $[-10,10]$, improves acceptance ratio compared to the standard EDF with $\lambda= 0$, especially for EQDF.
conclusions: choosing $\lambda$ to be the best integer in $[-10,10]$, improves acceptance ratio compared to the standard EDF with $\lambda= 0$, especially for EQDF

nodes.name: Neither window dominates in experiments
nodes.statement: We see that both the fixed and the variable analysis window lead to better acceptance ratios in certain scenarios, depending on the size of $x$ and the scheduling algorithm under analysis.
conclusions: both the fixed and the variable analysis window lead to better acceptance ratios in certain scenarios

nodes.name: Runtime with 200 tasks
nodes.statement: However, even with $200$ tasks per task set, our schedulability test takes on average $12.87$ seconds and at most $17.77$ seconds to return the result for one task set.
conclusions: even with $200$ tasks per task set, our schedulability test takes on average $12.87$ seconds and at most $17.77$ seconds to return the result for one task set

nodes.name: Assume EL and TFP schedules differ
nodes.statement: For an indirect proof we assume that the schedule of $\Tbb$ under EL and TFP does not coincide.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: Assume EL and TFP schedules differ

nodes.name: Pick highest-priority differing job, define interval I and job sets
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: Pick highest-priority differing job, define interval I and job sets

nodes.name: Plan: partition job sets by task group and compare each part
nodes.statement:
We will reach a contradiction by showing that $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}=\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}$ and that further the schedule of the jobs in $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}=\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}$ coincides under TFP and under EL scheduling.
	For that purpose we partition the job sets into three subsets
	$\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}} = \coprod_{i \in \setof{+, -, 0}} \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^i$ and
	$\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}} = \coprod_{i \in \setof{+, -, 0}} \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^i$,




	where each of them denotes the subset of jobs released by tasks of $\Tbb_{+} = \setof{\tau_{k+1}, \dots, \tau_n}$, $\Tbb_{-} = \setof{\tau_1, \dots, \tau_{k-1}}$ or $\Tbb_{0} = \setof{\tau_k}$.
	In the following we show that $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^i = \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^i$ for all $i \in \setof{+,-,0}$.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: Plan: partition job sets by task group and compare each part

nodes.name: Lower-priority tasks contribute no jobs
nodes.statement:
\paragraph{$\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^+ = \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^+$}

	Under TFP, there are no jobs of $\Tbb_{+}$ with higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$, i.e., $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^+ = \emptyset$.

	Under EL, we choose any job $\tau_{i,j}$, with $\tau_i \in \Tbb_{+}$, that has higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$, i.e., $\pi_{i,j}=r_{i,j} + \Pi_i \leq \pi_{k,\ell} = r_{k,\ell} + \Pi_k$ holds.
	By subtracting $\Pi_k$ we obtain
	\begin{equation} r_{i,j} + K_i \leq r_{i,j} + (\Pi_i-\Pi_k) \leq r_{k,\ell}.
	\end{equation}
 	Since $\tau_{i,j}$ has higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$, by assumption the schedule of $\tau_{i,j}$ coincides under EL and TFP, and we have $f_{i,j} \leq r_{i,j} + K_i$.
 	With Equation~\eqref{eq:pf_prop_TFPasEL_1} we conclude $f_{i,j} \leq r_{k,\ell}$.
 	In particular, the job $\tau_{i,j}$ is not executed during $I$.
 	Since $\tau_{i,j}$ was chosen arbitrarily, this means that $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^+ = \emptyset$ as well.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: Lower-priority tasks contribute no jobs

nodes.name: Under TFP no lower-priority-task job interferes
nodes.statement: Under TFP, there are no jobs of $\Tbb_{+}$ with higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$, i.e., $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^+ = \emptyset$.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: Under TFP no lower-priority-task job interferes

nodes.name: Under EL such jobs finish before r_{k,l}
nodes.statement:
Under EL, we choose any job $\tau_{i,j}$, with $\tau_i \in \Tbb_{+}$, that has higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$, i.e., $\pi_{i,j}=r_{i,j} + \Pi_i \leq \pi_{k,\ell} = r_{k,\ell} + \Pi_k$ holds.
	By subtracting $\Pi_k$ we obtain
	\begin{equation} r_{i,j} + K_i \leq r_{i,j} + (\Pi_i-\Pi_k) \leq r_{k,\ell}.
	\end{equation}
 	Since $\tau_{i,j}$ has higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$, by assumption the schedule of $\tau_{i,j}$ coincides under EL and TFP, and we have $f_{i,j} \leq r_{i,j} + K_i$.
 	With Equation~\eqref{eq:pf_prop_TFPasEL_1} we conclude $f_{i,j} \leq r_{k,\ell}$.
 	In particular, the job $\tau_{i,j}$ is not executed during $I$.
 	Since $\tau_{i,j}$ was chosen arbitrarily, this means that $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^+ = \emptyset$ as well.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: Under EL such jobs finish before r_{k,l}

nodes.name: Higher-priority tasks contribute the same jobs
nodes.statement:
\paragraph{$\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^- = \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^-$}
 	Under TFP and under EL, jobs of the tasks in $\Tbb_{-}$ 
 	can only be executed during $I$ if they are released before $r_{k,\ell} + K_k$, 
 	i.e., let $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$ be the set of jobs released before $r_{k,\ell} + K_k$ by tasks of $\Tbb_{-}$ then 
 	$\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^-, \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^- \subseteq \tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$.
 	Under TFP, all jobs in $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$ have higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$ since they are released by the tasks of $\Tbb_{-}$.
 	Under EL, we show the same:

 	Let $\tau_{i,j} \in \tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$, i.e., $r_{i,j} < r_{k,\ell} + K_k$.
 	It directly follows that
 	\begin{equation}
 		\pi_{i,j} = r_{i,j} + \Pi_i 
 		< r_{k,\ell} + K_k + \Pi_i
 		\leq r_{k,\ell} + \Pi_k = \pi_{k,\ell}.
 	\end{equation}
	In particular, $\tau_{i,j}$ has higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$.
	We have shown that all jobs in $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$ have higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$ under EL and under TFP scheduling.
	By assumption the schedule of the jobs in $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$ coincides under TFP and EL.
	Therefore the same jobs of $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$ executed during $I$ under TFP and EL, i.e., $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^- = \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^-$.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: Higher-priority tasks contribute the same jobs

nodes.name: Restrict to jobs released before r_{k,l}+K_k
nodes.statement:
Under TFP and under EL, jobs of the tasks in $\Tbb_{-}$ 
 	can only be executed during $I$ if they are released before $r_{k,\ell} + K_k$, 
 	i.e., let $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$ be the set of jobs released before $r_{k,\ell} + K_k$ by tasks of $\Tbb_{-}$ then 
 	$\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^-, \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^- \subseteq \tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$.
 	Under TFP, all jobs in $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$ have higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$ since they are released by the tasks of $\Tbb_{-}$.
 	Under EL, we show the same:
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to jobs released before r_{k,l}+K_k

nodes.name: Such jobs have higher priority under EL
nodes.statement:
Let $\tau_{i,j} \in \tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$, i.e., $r_{i,j} < r_{k,\ell} + K_k$.
 	It directly follows that
 	\begin{equation}
 		\pi_{i,j} = r_{i,j} + \Pi_i 
 		< r_{k,\ell} + K_k + \Pi_i
 		\leq r_{k,\ell} + \Pi_k = \pi_{k,\ell}.
 	\end{equation}
	In particular, $\tau_{i,j}$ has higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: Such jobs have higher priority under EL

nodes.name: Same jobs executed during I
nodes.statement:
We have shown that all jobs in $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$ have higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$ under EL and under TFP scheduling.
	By assumption the schedule of the jobs in $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$ coincides under TFP and EL.
	Therefore the same jobs of $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^-$ executed during $I$ under TFP and EL, i.e., $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^- = \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^-$.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: Same jobs executed during I

nodes.name: Earlier jobs of the same task coincide
nodes.statement:
\paragraph{$\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^0 = \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^0$}
	Under TFP and under EL, $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^0 := \setof{\tau_{k,1}, \dots, \tau_{k,\ell-1}}$ are the jobs of $\tau_k$ that have higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$, i.e., $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^0, \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^0 \subseteq \tilde{\mathbb{J}}^0$.
	By assumption, the schedule of the jobs in $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^0$ coincides.
	Therefore the same jobs of $\tilde{\mathbb{J}}^0$ are executed during $I$, i.e., we have $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}^0 = \mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}^0$.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: Earlier jobs of the same task coincide

nodes.name: Schedule of tau_{k,l} coincides, contradiction
nodes.statement:
We have shown that $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}=\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}$ by the above discussion.
	Since the schedule of the jobs $\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{TFP}}=\mathbb{J}_{\mathrm{EL}}$ coincides during $I$, $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is preempted/blocked during the same time intervals under TFP and EL scheduling during $I$.
	Hence, the schedule of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ during $I$ coincides.
	Furthermore, since by assumption $K_k$ is an upper bound on the response time under EL or TFP scheduling, the job $\tau_{k,\ell}$ finishes during $I$.
	This proves that the whole schedule of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ coincides.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: Schedule of tau_{k,l} coincides, contradiction

nodes.name: EL schedulability makes deadlines response-time bounds
nodes.statement: If $\Tbb$ is schedulable under EL with the given relative priority points $\Pi_i$, then $D_j$ is an upper bound on the worst-case response time of $\tau_j$ for all $\tau_j \in \Tbb$ under EL scheduling.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: EL schedulability makes deadlines response-time bounds

nodes.name: Apply Proposition 3
nodes.statement: In this case, by Proposition~\ref{prop:TFPasEL} the schedule under TFP and EL coincide.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 3

nodes.name: Deadlines bound TFP response times
nodes.statement:
Therefore, $D_j$ is also an upper bound on the worst-case response time of $\tau_j$ for all $\tau_j \in \Tbb$ under TFP scheduling.
	Hence, $\Tbb$ is schedulable under TFP as well.
nodes.section: 3 Capabilities and Limitations of EL Scheduling
nodes.statement_short: Deadlines bound TFP response times

nodes.name: Reduce to an equivalence of two conditions
nodes.statement:
The lemma follows from the equivalence between: 1)~the processor is in PS~2 and 
		2)~the processor is \emph{working on or suspended by some job of $\tau_k$ while it is not working on higher-priority jobs}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to an equivalence of two conditions

nodes.name: Work-conservation gives equivalence with current job
nodes.statement: Since the processor is work-conserving, we obtain an equivalence between 1) and \emph{the processor is working on or suspended by the current job of $\tau_k$ while it is not working on a higher-priority job}.
nodes.statement_short: Work-conservation gives equivalence with current job

nodes.name: Executing job is the current job
nodes.statement:
By the definition of the current job, if the processor is working on or suspended by a job, then this is the current job by default. 
		This concludes the equivalence between 1) and 2).
nodes.statement_short: Executing job is the current job

nodes.name: Translate both conditions into time amounts
nodes.statement: By definition, the time of 1) during $[c,d)$ is $B_k(c,d)$, and the time of 2) during $[c,d)$ is $\sum_{j \in \Nbb} B_{k,j}(c,d)$.
nodes.statement_short: Translate both conditions into time amounts

nodes.name: Recall the definition of PS 3 time
nodes.statement: By definition, $B^i_k(c,d)$ is the amount of time during $[c,d)$ that the processor is working on a job of $\tau_i$ with higher priority than the current job of $\tau_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the definition of PS 3 time

nodes.name: Equality when tau_{k,l} is current throughout
nodes.statement: If $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the current job of $\tau_k$ during the whole interval, then $B^i_k(c,d) = B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d)$.
nodes.statement_short: Equality when tau_{k,l} is current throughout

nodes.name: Inequality when tau_{k,l} is the last current job
nodes.statement:
If $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is current during $[d-\eps,d)$, then any job of $\tau_k$ which is current at some time during $[c,d)$ has a priority higher than or equal to the priority of $\tau_{k,\ell}$.
		If the processor is working on a job of $\tau_i$ with higher priority than the current job of $\tau_k$ at that time, then that job of $\tau_i$ has also higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$.
		As a result, $B^i_k(c,d) \leq B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d)$.
nodes.statement_short: Inequality when tau_{k,l} is the last current job

nodes.name: Decompose interval length via Lemmas 10 and 12
nodes.statement:
Since $\tau_k$ is active during $[c,d)$, we have $\widetilde{B}_k(c,d) = 0$.
		Using this together with Lemma~\ref{lem:distribution_ps_with_b} and Lemma~\ref{lem:refinement_Bk} leads to $\sum_{i\neq k} B^i_k(c,d) + \sum_{j\in\Nbb} B_{k,j}(c,d) = (d-c)$.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose interval length via Lemmas 10 and 12

nodes.name: Reduce to two inequalities
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to two inequalities

nodes.name: Prove inequality 1)
nodes.statement:
First, we prove 1). 
		Since $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is not finished by time $d$, we know that all $\tau_{k,j}$ with $j>\ell$ are not current before $d$.
		Hence, $B_{k,j}(c,d) = 0$ for all $j > \ell$ and $\sum_{j \in \Nbb} B_{k,j}(c,d) = \sum_{j \leq \ell} B_{k,j}(c,d)$.
		Moreover, due to Lemma~\ref{lem:Bkl_finished}, we have $B_{k,\ell}(c,d) < C_k+S_k$.
		This proves 1).
nodes.statement_short: Prove inequality 1)

nodes.name: Later jobs are never current before d
nodes.statement:
Since $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is not finished by time $d$, we know that all $\tau_{k,j}$ with $j>\ell$ are not current before $d$.
		Hence, $B_{k,j}(c,d) = 0$ for all $j > \ell$ and $\sum_{j \in \Nbb} B_{k,j}(c,d) = \sum_{j \leq \ell} B_{k,j}(c,d)$.
nodes.statement_short: Later jobs are never current before d

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 14
nodes.statement:
Moreover, due to Lemma~\ref{lem:Bkl_finished}, we have $B_{k,\ell}(c,d) < C_k+S_k$.
		This proves 1).
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 14

nodes.name: Prove inequality 2)
nodes.statement:
Second, we prove 2).
		Since $\tau_{k}$ is active during $[c,d)$, by definition, at any time instant $t \in [c, d)$, there is always a job of $\tau_k$, which is current. Let the last job of $\tau_k$ that is current in this interval be $\tau_{k,\ell'}$. That is, there exists some $\eps >0$ such that $\tau_{k,\ell'}$ is current during $[d-\eps,d)$.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:refinement_Bik}, we have $B^i_k(c,d) \leq B^i_{k,\ell'}(c,d)$ for all $i\neq k$.

        According to the handling mechanism to deal with multiple
        active jobs of $\tau_k$ (for arbitrary-deadline task systems) at the end of Section~\ref{sec:system_model}, the jobs of
        $\tau_k$ are executed one after another. Since
        $\tau_{k,\ell'}$ is current in $[d-\eps,d)$, the job
        $\tau_{k,\ell}$ can not have higher priority than
        $\tau_{k, \ell'}$, i.e., $\ell' \leq \ell$ holds.
        Otherwise,
        $\tau_{k,\ell}$ has to be finished by time $d-\eps$.
        Therefore, $B^i_{k,\ell'}(c,d) \leq B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d)$ for all
        $i\neq k$. 
        We conclude that 2) holds.
nodes.statement_short: Prove inequality 2)

nodes.name: Last current job and Lemma 13
nodes.statement: Since $\tau_{k}$ is active during $[c,d)$, by definition, at any time instant $t \in [c, d)$, there is always a job of $\tau_k$, which is current. Let the last job of $\tau_k$ that is current in this interval be $\tau_{k,\ell'}$. That is, there exists some $\eps >0$ such that $\tau_{k,\ell'}$ is current during $[d-\eps,d)$.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:refinement_Bik}, we have $B^i_k(c,d) \leq B^i_{k,\ell'}(c,d)$ for all $i\neq k$.
nodes.statement_short: Last current job and Lemma 13

nodes.name: FIFO mechanism gives l' <= l
nodes.statement:
According to the handling mechanism to deal with multiple
        active jobs of $\tau_k$ (for arbitrary-deadline task systems) at the end of Section~\ref{sec:system_model}, the jobs of
        $\tau_k$ are executed one after another. Since
        $\tau_{k,\ell'}$ is current in $[d-\eps,d)$, the job
        $\tau_{k,\ell}$ can not have higher priority than
        $\tau_{k, \ell'}$, i.e., $\ell' \leq \ell$ holds.
        Otherwise,
        $\tau_{k,\ell}$ has to be finished by time $d-\eps$.
nodes.statement_short: FIFO mechanism gives l' <= l

nodes.name: Monotonicity in the job index
nodes.statement:
Therefore, $B^i_{k,\ell'}(c,d) \leq B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d)$ for all
        $i\neq k$. 
        We conclude that 2) holds.
nodes.statement_short: Monotonicity in the job index

nodes.name: Assume tau_{k,l} unfinished at d
nodes.statement: We use an indirect proof strategy and assume that $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is not finished by time $d$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume tau_{k,l} unfinished at d

nodes.name: tau_k active throughout [c,d)
nodes.statement:
In this case, $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is active during $[r_{k,\ell},d)$.
		Since $r_{k,\ell}\leq c$ or $\tau_k$ is active during $[c,r_{k,\ell})$, we conclude that $\tau_k$ is also active during $[c,d)$.
nodes.statement_short: tau_k active throughout [c,d)

nodes.name: Lemma 15 contradicts the hypothesis
nodes.statement:
Lemma~\ref{lem:non-sched} states that Equation~\eqref{eq:prop:backbone_prep} does not hold.
		This contradicts our assumption.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 15 contradicts the hypothesis

nodes.name: Instantiate Proposition 16 with d
nodes.statement:
This corollary follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:backbone_prep} by setting $d:=r_{k,\ell} + \widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$.
		The case $c>d$ does not occur since otherwise $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} \geq  c-r_{k,\ell} > \widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ would hold by definition of $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ and $d$.
		We only consider $c \leq d$.
nodes.statement_short: Instantiate Proposition 16 with d

nodes.name: Bound the B terms by those over [c,d_{k,l})
nodes.statement:
Since $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} \leq D_k$ by assumption, we have $d\leq d_{k,\ell}$.
		Hence, $B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d)\leq B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d_{k,\ell})$ and $B_{k,j}(c,d) \leq B_{k,j}(c,d_{k,\ell})$ for all $i$ and all $j$.
		As a result, the left hand side of Equation~\eqref{eq:prop:backbone_prep} is less than or equal to $(C_k+ S_k) + \sum_{i \neq k} B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d_{k,\ell}) + \sum_{j < \ell} B_{k,j}(c,d_{k,\ell})$, which is the same as $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} + r_{k,\ell} - c = d-c$ by definition.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the B terms by those over [c,d_{k,l})

nodes.name: Conclude response-time bound
nodes.statement:
Since all assumptions from Proposition~\ref{prop:backbone_prep} hold, the job $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is finished by time $d=\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} + r_{k,\ell}$.
		Hence, $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ is an upper bound on the response time of $\tau_{k,\ell}$.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude response-time bound

nodes.name: Release window of relevant jobs
nodes.statement:
A job of $\tau_i$ can only be executed during $[c,d_{k,\ell})$, if it is released after $c-\widetilde{R}_i$.
		Moreover, it can have higher priority than $\tau_{k,\ell}$, if it is released no later than $r_{k,\ell} + \Pi_k - \Pi_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Release window of relevant jobs

nodes.name: Count releases in the window
nodes.statement:
We count the maximal number of releases of $\tau_i$ during $(c-\widetilde{R}_i, r_{k,\ell} + \Pi_k - \Pi_i)$ by $\ceiling{\frac{r_{k,\ell} + \Pi_k - \Pi_i - c + \widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}}$ if the interval has non-negative length.
		Otherwise, the number of releases is $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Count releases in the window

nodes.name: No interfering job: bound trivial
nodes.statement: If there is no job of $\tau_i$ executed during $[c,d_{k,\ell})$, then $B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d_{k,\ell})=0$ and the lemma is proven.
nodes.statement_short: No interfering job: bound trivial

nodes.name: Otherwise isolate the last interfering job
nodes.statement:
Otherwise, let $\tau_{i,j'}$ be the last job of $\tau_i$ being executed during $[c,d_{k,\ell})$.
		We isolate that job in the following way.
		Let $r_{i,j'}$ be the release time of $\tau_{i,j'}$ and let $C^*$ be the amount of time that the processor is working on $\tau_{i,j'}$ during the interval $[c,d_{k,\ell})$.
		We have $B(c,d_{k,\ell}) \leq B(c,r_{i,j'}) + C^*.$



		
		If $r_{i,j'}-c < (C-C^*)$, then $B(c,r_{i,j'}) + C^* \leq C$.
		Moreover, $\ceiling{\frac{D_k-C_i+r_{k,\ell}-c+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}}C_i \geq \ceiling{\frac{D_k+r_{k,\ell}-c}{T_i}}C_i \geq C_i$ since there is a job being executed during $[c, d_{k,\ell})$, i.e., $c < D_k+r_{k,\ell}$.
		In this case the lemma is proven.
		
		If $r_{i,j'}-c \geq (C-C^*)$, then $B(c,r_{i,j'}) + C^* \leq B(c + (C_i-C^*),r_{i,j'}) + C_i$, i.e., we over approximate be replacing $(C_i-C^*)$ time units at the beginning by execution time.
		Next we compute $B(c + (C_i-C^*),r_{i,j'})$ by counting the number of releases during the interval $(c+(C_i-C^*)-\widetilde{R}_i, r_{i,j'}-T_i]$.
		It is 

		$
			\ceiling{\frac{r_{i,j'}-T_i-c-C_i+C*+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}} 
			\leq \ceiling{\frac{r_{k,\ell}-T_i-c-C_i+D_k+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}}
			= \ceiling{\frac{r_{k,\ell}-c-C_i+D_k+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}} -1
		$

		where we use that $r_{i,j'} + C^* \leq r_{k,\ell} + D_k$.
		In total, the value of $B(c,d_{k,\ell})$ is then upper bounded by $\ceiling{\frac{r_{k,\ell}-c-C_i+D_k+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}} \cdot C_i$ in this case.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise isolate the last interfering job

nodes.name: Isolate last job and its execution C*
nodes.statement:
Otherwise, let $\tau_{i,j'}$ be the last job of $\tau_i$ being executed during $[c,d_{k,\ell})$.
		We isolate that job in the following way.
		Let $r_{i,j'}$ be the release time of $\tau_{i,j'}$ and let $C^*$ be the amount of time that the processor is working on $\tau_{i,j'}$ during the interval $[c,d_{k,\ell})$.
		We have $B(c,d_{k,\ell}) \leq B(c,r_{i,j'}) + C^*.$
nodes.statement_short: Isolate last job and its execution C*

nodes.name: Short prefix case
nodes.statement:
If $r_{i,j'}-c < (C-C^*)$, then $B(c,r_{i,j'}) + C^* \leq C$.
		Moreover, $\ceiling{\frac{D_k-C_i+r_{k,\ell}-c+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}}C_i \geq \ceiling{\frac{D_k+r_{k,\ell}-c}{T_i}}C_i \geq C_i$ since there is a job being executed during $[c, d_{k,\ell})$, i.e., $c < D_k+r_{k,\ell}$.
		In this case the lemma is proven.
nodes.statement_short: Short prefix case

nodes.name: Long prefix case: count releases
nodes.statement:
If $r_{i,j'}-c \geq (C-C^*)$, then $B(c,r_{i,j'}) + C^* \leq B(c + (C_i-C^*),r_{i,j'}) + C_i$, i.e., we over approximate be replacing $(C_i-C^*)$ time units at the beginning by execution time.
		Next we compute $B(c + (C_i-C^*),r_{i,j'})$ by counting the number of releases during the interval $(c+(C_i-C^*)-\widetilde{R}_i, r_{i,j'}-T_i]$.
		It is 

		$
			\ceiling{\frac{r_{i,j'}-T_i-c-C_i+C*+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}} 
			\leq \ceiling{\frac{r_{k,\ell}-T_i-c-C_i+D_k+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}}
			= \ceiling{\frac{r_{k,\ell}-c-C_i+D_k+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}} -1
		$

		where we use that $r_{i,j'} + C^* \leq r_{k,\ell} + D_k$.
		In total, the value of $B(c,d_{k,\ell})$ is then upper bounded by $\ceiling{\frac{r_{k,\ell}-c-C_i+D_k+\widetilde{R}_i}{T_i}} \cdot C_i$ in this case.
nodes.statement_short: Long prefix case: count releases

nodes.name: Set up induction over jobs ordered by priority
nodes.statement:
Assume we have found $b_k,~k=1,\dots,n$ such that Equation~\eqref{eq:suff_sched_test_fixed} holds.
		We consider some schedule obtained by this task set and denote by $Seq$ the sequence of all jobs in the schedule ordered by their priority.
		Via induction, we prove that the first $\xi$ jobs in $Seq$ have the required response time upper bound, for all $\xi \in \Nbb_0$.
		Consequently, $\widetilde{R}_k$ is an upper bound on the worst-case response time of $\tau_k$ for all $k$ and the task set is schedulable.
nodes.statement_short: Set up induction over jobs ordered by priority

nodes.name: Base case: empty set
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Initial case:} $\xi = 0$.
		In this case, the set of the first $\xi$ jobs in $Seq$ is $\{\}$ the empty set.
		Trivially, all of them have the required response time upper bound.
nodes.statement_short: Base case: empty set

nodes.name: Inductive step via Analysis Backbone
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Induction step:} $\xi \to \xi+1$.
		By assumption, the first $\xi$ jobs in $Seq$ have the required response time upper bound.
		We denote the $(\xi+1)$-th job in $Seq$ by $\tau_{k,\ell}$.
		We aim to use Corollary~\ref{cor:backbone} to prove that the response time of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is upper bounded by $\widetilde{R}_k$.
		
		By definition, we have $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} = (C_k+ S_k) + \sum_{i \neq k} B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d_{k,\ell}) + \sum_{j < \ell} B_{k,j}(c,d_{k,\ell}) + c - r_{k,\ell}$.
		Since all higher priority jobs have the required response time upper bound, we can use the estimation from Section~\ref{sec:estimation_B}.
		Using Lemma~\ref{lem:upper_bound_sum_Bkj} and Lemma~\ref{lem:total_bound_interference}, we obtain $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} \leq \widetilde{R}_k$ when choosing $c:= b_k+r_{k,\ell}$.
		Due to Equation~\eqref{eq:suff_sched_test_fixed}, even
		$\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} \leq \widetilde{R}_k \leq D_k$.



		We use Corollary~\ref{cor:backbone} to conclude that $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ is an upper bound on the response time of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ and therefore $\widetilde{R}_k$ is an upper bound on the response time of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step via Analysis Backbone

nodes.name: Take the next job tau_{k,l}
nodes.statement:
By assumption, the first $\xi$ jobs in $Seq$ have the required response time upper bound.
		We denote the $(\xi+1)$-th job in $Seq$ by $\tau_{k,\ell}$.
		We aim to use Corollary~\ref{cor:backbone} to prove that the response time of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is upper bounded by $\widetilde{R}_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the next job tau_{k,l}

nodes.name: Bound R_{k,l} with Bounds B1 and B2
nodes.statement:
By definition, we have $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} = (C_k+ S_k) + \sum_{i \neq k} B^i_{k,\ell}(c,d_{k,\ell}) + \sum_{j < \ell} B_{k,j}(c,d_{k,\ell}) + c - r_{k,\ell}$.
		Since all higher priority jobs have the required response time upper bound, we can use the estimation from Section~\ref{sec:estimation_B}.
		Using Lemma~\ref{lem:upper_bound_sum_Bkj} and Lemma~\ref{lem:total_bound_interference}, we obtain $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} \leq \widetilde{R}_k$ when choosing $c:= b_k+r_{k,\ell}$.
		Due to Equation~\eqref{eq:suff_sched_test_fixed}, even
		$\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell} \leq \widetilde{R}_k \leq D_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound R_{k,l} with Bounds B1 and B2

nodes.name: Conclude with the Analysis Backbone
nodes.statement: We use Corollary~\ref{cor:backbone} to conclude that $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ is an upper bound on the response time of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ and therefore $\widetilde{R}_k$ is an upper bound on the response time of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude with the Analysis Backbone

nodes.name: Apply the Analysis Backbone
nodes.statement: For the proof, we apply Corollary~\ref{cor:backbone}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Analysis Backbone

nodes.name: Choice of c satisfies the backbone restriction
nodes.statement:
Since $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the $(a+1)$-th job in an active interval, $\tau_k$ is active during $[r_{k,\ell-a}, r_{k,\ell})$.
		Hence, the restriction on $c$ in Corollary~\ref{cor:backbone} are fulfilled by default, when $c$ is chosen from $[r_{k,\ell-a}, d_{k,\ell})$.
nodes.statement_short: Choice of c satisfies the backbone restriction

nodes.name: Self-interference at most a(C_k+S_k)
nodes.statement:
Moreover, since $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the $(a+1)$-th job in an active interval, the jobs $\tau_{k,1}, \dots, \tau_{k,\ell-a-1}$ are finished by time $r_{k,\ell-a}$.
		We obtain $\sum_{j < \ell-a} B_{k,j} (c,d_{k,\ell}) \leq \sum_{j < \ell-a} B_{k,j} (r_{k,\ell-a},d_{k,\ell}) = 0$.
		Hence, 

		$
			\sum_{j < \ell} B_{k,j} (c,d_{k,\ell}) 
			= \sum_{j = \ell-a}^{\ell-1} B_{k,j} (c,d_{k,\ell})
			\leq \sum_{j = \ell-a}^{\ell-1} (C_k+S_k)
			= a\cdot (C_k+S_k).

		$
nodes.statement_short: Self-interference at most a(C_k+S_k)

nodes.name: Combine with Bound B2 and conclude
nodes.statement:
We combine this with the results from Lemma~\ref{lem:upper_bound_sum_Bkj} and Lemma~\ref{lem:total_bound_interference}, and obtain that $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ from Equation~\eqref{eq:cor_sched_test} is less than or equal to the value in Equation~\eqref{eq:lem_var_window}.
		If \eqref{eq:lem_var_window} is at most $D_k$, then $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}\leq D_k$.
		Corollary~\ref{cor:backbone} states that $\widetilde{R}_{k,\ell}$ is an upper bound on the response time of $r_{k,\ell}$ and therefore, also \eqref{eq:lem_var_window} is an upper bound on the response time.
nodes.statement_short: Combine with Bound B2 and conclude

nodes.name: Induction plan with two bounds
nodes.statement:
The proof is similar to the one of Theorem~\ref{thm:suff_sched_test_fixed}.
		Let $Seq$ be the sequence of all jobs in the schedule ordered by their priority.
		By induction we show that the following response time upper bound holds for the first $\xi \in \Nbb_0$ jobs in $Seq$:
nodes.statement_short: Induction plan with two bounds

nodes.name: Bound 1: R_k for all jobs
nodes.statement: $\widetilde{R}_k$ for all jobs of $\tau_k$ for each task $\tau_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound 1: R_k for all jobs

nodes.name: Bound 2: T_k for tilde-a-th jobs
nodes.statement: $T_k$ for all $\tilde a_k$-th jobs in an active interval of $\tau_k$ for each task $\tau_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound 2: T_k for tilde-a-th jobs

nodes.name: Base case trivial
nodes.statement: \textbf{Initial case:} $\xi_0$. The initial case is again trivially fulfilled, since there has nothing to be checked when there are no jobs.
nodes.statement_short: Base case trivial

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement:
\textbf{Induction step:} $\xi \to \xi+1$.
		The first $\xi$ jobs in $Seq$ have the required response time upper bounds 1) and 2) by induction.
		We denote by $\tau_{k,\ell}$ the $(\xi+1)$-th job of $Seq$.
		Let $a$ be the lowest value in $\Nbb_0$, such that $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the $(a+1)$-th job in an active interval of $\tau_k$.
		We first show that $a\leq \tilde a_k$ by contraposition.
		If $a > \tilde a$, then we consider the job $\tau_{k,\ell-(a-\tilde a)}$.
		This is the $(\tilde a+1)$-th job in an active interval of $\tau_k$.
		Moreover, this job is one of the first $\xi$ jobs in $Seq$ and therefore has a response time of at most $T_k$ due to 2).
		Hence, $\tau_{k,\ell-(a-\tilde a)}$ is finished by time $r_{k,\ell-(a-\tilde a)+1}$.
		We conclude that $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the $(a-\tilde a_k)$-th job in an active interval of $\tau_k$, which contradicts the minimality of $a$.
		We now choose $c:=b^a_k-a\cdot T_k + r_{k,\ell}$.
		Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:suff_sched_test_var_prep} with this $c$ shows that $\widetilde{R}^a_k(b^a_k)$ is a response time upper bound of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ as required.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step

The first $\xi$ jobs in $Seq$ have the required response time upper bounds 1) and 2) by induction.
		We denote by $\tau_{k,\ell}$ the $(\xi+1)$-th job of $Seq$.

		Hence, $\tau_{k,\ell-(a-\tilde a)}$ is finished by time $r_{k,\ell-(a-\tilde a)+1}$.
		We conclude that $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the $(a-\tilde a_k)$-th job in an active interval of $\tau_k$, which contradicts the minimality of $a$.

nodes.name: Consider the (tilde a+1)-th job
nodes.statement:
If $a > \tilde a$, then we consider the job $\tau_{k,\ell-(a-\tilde a)}$.
		This is the $(\tilde a+1)$-th job in an active interval of $\tau_k$.
		Moreover, this job is one of the first $\xi$ jobs in $Seq$ and therefore has a response time of at most $T_k$ due to 2).

nodes.name: It finishes before next release, contradiction
nodes.statement:
Hence, $\tau_{k,\ell-(a-\tilde a)}$ is finished by time $r_{k,\ell-(a-\tilde a)+1}$.
		We conclude that $\tau_{k,\ell}$ is the $(a-\tilde a_k)$-th job in an active interval of $\tau_k$, which contradicts the minimality of $a$.
nodes.statement_short: It finishes before next release, contradiction

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 25 with chosen c
nodes.statement:
We now choose $c:=b^a_k-a\cdot T_k + r_{k,\ell}$.
		Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:suff_sched_test_var_prep} with this $c$ shows that $\widetilde{R}^a_k(b^a_k)$ is a response time upper bound of $\tau_{k,\ell}$ as required.

nodes.name: Reason 1: bounded active intervals required
nodes.statement:
First, the analysis with variable analysis window can only analyze schedules where the length of active intervals is bounded.
More specifically, if the response-time upper bound $\widetilde{R}^a_k$ is in the interval $(T_k, D_k)$ for all $a$, then the schedulability test with the variable analysis window never deems the task schedulable.
nodes.section: 4.5 Dominance of Fixed and Variable Analysis Window
nodes.statement_short: Reason 1: bounded active intervals required

nodes.name: Reason 2: max_a intensifies the effect
nodes.statement:
Second, by setting $max\_a$ this effect is even intensified:
The analysis with variable analysis window has to find $\widetilde{R}^a_k \leq T_k$ even for some $a \leq max\_a$.
nodes.section: 4.5 Dominance of Fixed and Variable Analysis Window
nodes.statement_short: Reason 2: max_a intensifies the effect

nodes.name: Reason 3: discretization checks different points
nodes.statement:
Third, the discretization using $\eta$ in Algorithm~\ref{alg:sched_test_fixed} and~\ref{alg:sched_test_var} ensures the same number of points for each analysis interval.
As a result, not all points $b+aT_k$ with $b$ from Algorithm~\ref{alg:sched_test_fixed} are checked during Algorithm~\ref{alg:sched_test_var} as well.
nodes.section: 4.5 Dominance of Fixed and Variable Analysis Window
nodes.statement_short: Reason 3: discretization checks different points

nodes.name: On arrival, select and run the highest-priority job
nodes.statement: when a job is added to the ready queue, the new highest-priority job is determined and executed.
nodes.statement_short: On arrival, select and run the highest-priority job

nodes.name: On finish or suspension, remove job and reselect
nodes.statement: Whenever a job finishes or suspends itself, it is removed from the ready queue and a new highest-priority job has to be determined and is executed.
nodes.statement_short: On finish or suspension, remove job and reselect

nodes.name: Map job priority to its absolute deadline at release
nodes.statement: At each job release, its priority should be identified with its absolute deadline, and necessary priority mapping operations should be performed.
nodes.statement_short: Map job priority to its absolute deadline at release

nodes.name: Insert job into priority-ordered ready queue
nodes.statement: The job context is placed into the ready queue according to its priority, which is commonly realized by a dedicated data structure, e.g., a red-black tree in RTEMS and a binomial heap in {$\text{LITMUS}^{\text{RT}}$}.
nodes.statement_short: Insert job into priority-ordered ready queue

nodes.name: Run a highest-priority job, resolving ties
nodes.statement: One highest priority job should be executed. In case there are deadline ties, a regulation should be performed. This step also takes place if a job finishes its execution.
nodes.statement_short: Run a highest-priority job, resolving ties

nodes.name: 500 task sets per utilization level, 50 tasks each
nodes.statement:
For the experiments, we synthesize $500$ task sets for each utilization from $0\%$ to $100\%$ in steps of $5\%$.
	For each task set we generate $50$ tasks.
nodes.statement_short: 500 task sets per utilization level, 50 tasks each

nodes.name: Draw utilizations with UUniFast and periods log-uniformly
nodes.statement: We first generate $50$ utilization values $U_i$ using the UUniFast~\cite{DBLP:journals/rts/BiniB05} method with the given total utilization goal, and then adopt the suggestion by Emberson~et~al.~\cite{emberson2010techniques} to pull the minimum inter-arrival time $T_i$ according to a log-uniform distribution from the interval $[1,100] [ms]$.
nodes.statement_short: Draw utilizations with UUniFast and periods log-uniformly

nodes.name: Set WCET from utilization and implicit deadlines
nodes.statement: The worst-case execution time is computed by $C_i = T_i \cdot U_i$ and the deadline is set to the minimum inter-arrival time $D_i = T_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Set WCET from utilization and implicit deadlines

nodes.name: Draw suspension times uniformly
nodes.statement: For each task, we draw the maximum suspension time $S_i$ uniformly at random from $[0,0.5(T_i-C_i)]$.
nodes.statement_short: Draw suspension times uniformly
